records.title: SynDebug: A Framework to Debug Logic Bugs in Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Programs
authors: Nick DiBrita    Jack Lange    Tirthak Patel
records.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) introduces substantial systems-level complexity through quantum error correction (QEC), making debugging FTQC programs challenging. Existing quantum debugging approaches primarily target logical-level circuits and do not naturally support debugging within realistic FTQC execution flows. We present SynDebug, the first systems-level debugging framework for FTQC programs. SynDebug introduces lightweight assertion-based debugging primitives that operate directly within encoded FTQC infrastructures while avoiding additional logical surface area and minimizing temporal overhead. We evaluate SynDebug across multiple QEC code families, code distances, and encoded workloads, including state preparation, entanglement validation, and Shor-style programs. Our results demonstrate that SynDebug enables practical FTQC debugging with an average 1.8% additional circuit depth overhead (0% in most cases) and no measurable increase in the logical error rate, showing that systems-level debugging for large-scale FTQC applications is both feasible and practical.

records.title: Detecting and Localizing Network Faults in RoCE-Based AI Clouds under Restricted Telemetry
records.abstract: This paper addresses network fault detection and localization in Huawei’s large-scale RoCE-based AI public cloud infrastructures. Diagnosing network faults is difficult in this scenario. Public-cloud privacy and commodity-switch hardware restrict the available diagnostic signals to network-side, standard-switch telemetry. Moreover, RoCE semantics and the throughput-sensitive training workloads we host make TCP-targeted and latency-based techniques a poor fit. To address these challenges, we present FACT, a production system that exploits protocol-native signals already present in the network using only commodity-switch capabilities. These signals include NAK packets for packet loss, packet conservation counters, and per-flow throughput computed from mirrored packet headers. FACT organizes these signals into a two-tier architecture that separates objective fault detection from evidence-based root-cause analysis. We have deployed FACT in multiple production infrastructures, and the longest deployment has lasted 18 months. Across all deployed infrastructures in 2025, FACT detected thousands of network faults and localized 99.95% of network faults within 10 minutes.

records.title: SptcAttn: Accelerating Long-Context Attention with Diagonal Stripes using Sparse Tensor Core
authors: Qiqi Gu    Heng Shi    Jianguo Yao
records.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is increasingly bottlenecked by attention, whose computational cost grows quadratically with sequence length. To alleviate this, recent research has proposed various sparse attention methods that compute only the important regions of the attention matrix. However, on GPUs, this selection operates at block granularity, where each block is either fully computed or entirely skipped. Blocks that partially overlap the selected regions still compute all entries inside them, introducing redundant work. We observe that this redundancy is not random but inherits the geometric structure of the selected pattern, creating an opportunity for hardware-accelerated sparse execution. We present SptcAttn, a system that exploits this band structure by losslessly mapping it to the 2:4 structured sparsity format of Sparse Tensor Cores (SpTCs), without discarding any score selected by the sparse attention pattern. SptcAttn combines three mechanisms: (1) a deterministic column permutation that converts band matrices into SpTC-compatible layout, (2) a block pair selection strategy that constructs well-formed band tiles from diagonal stripes without tile overlap, and (3) kernel integration that absorbs the permutation and metadata preparation into the fused FlashAttention pipeline without explicit data movement. SptcAttn achieves up to 1.55 × kernel speedup over the fastest existing sparse kernel. In end-to-end prefill, it preserves the accuracy of the underlying sparse-attention method and achieves an additional 1.06 × –1.08 × speedup over MInference for sequence lengths of 200K–500K, with a 6.58 × speedup over the dense-attention baseline at a sequence length of 500K.

records.title: DESAN: READ/WRITE-Aware Redundant Sanitizer Check Elimination
records.abstract: Sanitizers such as ASan, UBSan, and MSan are widely used to detect memory-related errors and undefined behavior. However, their high runtime overhead makes continuous use difficult in testing and production-like executions. A major source of this overhead is redundant sanitizer instrumentation: compiler-inserted checks often validate the same variable repeatedly along the same control-flow paths. Reducing sanitizer checks requires reasoning about the property each check validates and the program state on which it depends. We explore a conservative policy that eliminates only covered READ checks and retains WRITE checks and those whose semantics remain unresolved. This paper presents DeSan, an LLVM IR-level framework that reduces redundant sanitizer checks while preserving sanitizer semantics. DeSan identifies high-impact core checks and recovers the checked variable for each check through backward IR tracing. It then classifies checks as READ, WRITE, or UNKNOWN and builds per-variable check graphs to find covered READ checks. DeSan preserves all WRITE and UNKNOWN checks. When safe, it removes redundant READ checks along with their sanitizer-only IR slices, including shadow computation, comparisons, branches, and isolated report paths. We evaluate DeSan on SPEC CPU2006, SPEC CPU2017, and 20 open-source projects. Across 163 valid sanitizer configurations, core checks cover a median of 96.62% of inserted checks, and DeSan removes a median of 51.48% of all checks while preserving evaluated bug-detection capability. Compared with ASAN− − for ASan and SanRazor for UBSan, DeSan achieves competitive or stronger overhead reduction.

records.title: LiveART: Scaling WebRTC Ingestion
authors: Jianlin Xu    Bo Wang    Sandesh Dhawaskar Sathyanarayana    Wei Cao
Liang Yin    Feng Qian    Shu Shi
records.abstract: This paper introduces LiveART, a WebRTC-based transport ingest system designed for the first-mile ingestion of large-scale live streaming services. LiveART addresses the QoE (Quality of Experience) gaps that RTMP (Real-Time Messaging Protocol) struggles to meet amid growing demands for low-latency live streaming. We share our experience of integrating WebRTC into large-scale live streaming systems, where cost, QoE, and computational load are critical. Our experimental studies reveal that direct integration of WebRTC harms user engagement due to mismatched QoS settings and bitrate oscillations, and incurs operational bandwidth overhead from an elevated bitrate. To overcome these hurdles, LiveART adapts standard WebRTC to large-scale ingestion transport through a series of pragmatic, non-intrusive designs across multi-level QoS enhancements, transport-level stability, and media-layer perception-guided bitrate control. Production A/B tests involving 480K streamers and over 4.8 billion views prove that LiveART significantly outperforms the RTMP protocol. Compared to RTMP, LiveART significantly improves QoE, reducing rebuffering time and frequency by 10.1% and 12.42%, audio stall time and frequency by 17.84% and 18.45%, video stall time and frequency by 5.94% and 6.44%, and end-to-end latency by 2.55%, while increasing bitrate by 1.49%. Additionally, LiveART reduces bandwidth costs by 1.46% during peak hours, while maintaining user engagement. Finally, ablation studies and a subjective user study (446 participants, 13,380 ratings) comprehensively validate the efficacy of LiveART’s design.

records.title: PAVE: Prebuilding Address Translations for Fast Nested MicroVM Restore
records.abstract: Nested virtualization lets serverless platforms run MicroVM-based function runtimes on virtualized cloud infrastructure, but it makes snapshot restore substantially more expensive. Existing systems either overlap snapshot-page loading with execution to achieve data readiness , or reduce the cost of individual nested EPT faults. However, neither makes final nested translations ready before restored pages are first touched. Nested KVM still constructs these translations reactively, one page at a time, on the synchronous first-touch path, causing severe latency under high-concurrency same-snapshot restore bursts. We present PAVE , a nested-hypervisor extension that makes translation readiness a first-class restore objective. PAVE combines two mechanisms. Latency-hidden EPT prebuilding uses recorded working-set and snapshot metadata to construct validated final nested translations at L0 concurrently with MicroVM execution; if a MicroVM reaches a page first, the L0 fault handler installs the same translation directly, avoiding the normal nested fault path through L1. Cross-VM EPT sharing places clean, non-writable translations in a snapshot-scoped shared EPT hierarchy so that MicroVMs restored from the same snapshot can reuse them without repeated construction. PAVE preserves isolation with a simple invariant—shared EPT entries are append-only and non-writable—and routes writes through per-VM copy-on-write EPT overlays without cross-VM TLB shootdowns. Our evaluation on serverless benchmarks shows that PAVE reduces high-concurrency restore latency by 7.11 × over FaaSnap-Nested and by 3.23 × over FaaSnap+HT .

records.title: TensorBridge: Bridging Microscaled FP4 Weights to FP8 Tensor Cores for LLM Serving
records.abstract: Low-bit LLM serving increasingly targets W4A8 execution, where 4-bit weights reduce memory traffic while 8-bit activations retain a high-throughput Tensor Core path. NVFP4 is an attractive checkpoint format for this regime because its E2M1 payloads and group-16 E4M3 scales preserve accuracy better than coarse integer W4 formats. However, deployed GPUs without native NVFP4 Tensor Core support cannot execute these checkpoints as stored. Keeping these checkpoints on such GPUs falls back to A16 execution and misses the FP8 Tensor Core path. Converting them offline to FP8 or integer W4A8 recovers that path, but either doubles weight traffic or gives up NVFP4’s accuracy advantage. This paper presents TensorBridge, a software-defined NVFP4A8 execution path for native NVFP4 checkpoints on Hopper GPUs. TensorBridge treats NVFP4-to-FP8 translation as register-level WGMMA operand construction rather than checkpoint conversion or expanded-weight materialization. Because Hopper’s CUDA cores lack FP8 multipliers, it exploits floating-point multiplication approximation (FPMA) to turn E2M1-by-E4M3 scaling into CUDA-core integer shift-and-add operations. These CUDA-core operations construct FP8-compatible operands directly in registers, so Tensor Cores stay dedicated to FP8 WGMMA. TensorBridge reaches 71.98% average zero-shot accuracy, only 0.28 points below BF16 and 0.59 points above W4A8. It outperforms vLLM CUTLASS W4A8 by 1.15 × and NVFP4A16 Marlin by 2.62 × geometric mean. TensorBridge is open-sourced at https://github.com/CLab-HKUST-GZ/atc26-tensorbridge.

records.title: Mosaic: Efficient CPU–GPU Coordinated Block-Sparse Attention for Long-Context Decoding
authors: Feiyu Yao    Zhixiong Niu    Xiaqing Li    Yongqiang Xiong    Juan Fang
records.abstract: Long-context LLM serving increasingly relies on CPU-resident context KV cache, driven by KV offloading and disaggregated prefill–decode execution. Although block-sparse attention reduces KV access, existing designs remain inefficient: GPU-centralized execution fetches selected KV blocks from CPU memory at each decoding step, making it PCIe-bound, while CPU–GPU partitioned execution places CPU-side sparse attention on the critical path, leaving substantial GPU time idle. This paper presents Mosaic, a CPU–GPU coordinated block-sparse attention system for efficient long-context decoding with CPU-resident context KV. Mosaic builds on three key insights: output-contribution-aware KV budgeting, head-specific and granularity-aware sparse configuration, and cross-device coordinated scheduling for sparse tasks over CPU-resident KV. Guided by these insights, Mosaic integrates a lightweight head-property predictor, a granularity–budget selector, and a priority-based scheduler to automatically configure and coordinate sparse attention, preserving output quality while improving efficiency on heterogeneous architectures. Across 2 models, 3 benchmarks, and 40 tasks, Mosaic preserves near-FULL quality while achieving a better overall quality–efficiency tradeoff than the evaluated baselines. Compared with the best-quality fixed Quest configuration, Mosaic improves TPOT by up to 3.7 ×. We further validate Mosaic across four hardware configurations and in a large-model multi-GPU deployment.

records.title: Fine-Grained Loss Recovery via Packet-Level Content-Awareness for Ultra-low-latency Video Communications
authors: Wei Li    Zhewen Yang    Hua Meng
records.abstract: Ultra-low-latency video applications, such as cloud gaming and VR, increasingly deliver high-bitrate frames within tens of milliseconds. As each frame may contain hundreds of packets, uniformly retransmitting every lost packet can unnecessarily block an entire frame, even when the missing packet has little rendered-quality impact. This paper presents LetItGo , a receiver-side content-aware loss-recovery mechanism based on the observation that lost packets within the same frame can have very different impacts on frame quality. LetItGo uses packet position and pre-decoding to decide whether a lost packet is worth waiting for. It retransmits high-impact losses and lets the existing decoder conceal less critical ones, enabling fine-grained recovery without changing the sender, encoder, playback-decoder interface, or transport protocol. We implement LetItGo in WebRTC for H.264 and extend it to H.265. Experiments with high-resolution videos and real cloud-gaming traces show that LetItGo reduces transmission time by 9.41% on average over a strong loss-recovery baseline while keeping rendered quality within a 0.44 dB-SSIM gap. Results across H.264 and H.265 at both 30 and 60 fps show that the benefit is not tied to a single codec.

records.title: SOLO: Making Single-Local-Replica Storage Practical for Geo-Distributed Recommendation Model Training
records.abstract: Large-scale deep learning recommendation model (DLRM) training commonly spans geo-distributed datacenters. Modern DLRMs consume increasingly rich training samples, pushing data footprints toward exabyte scale. At this scale, maintaining local storage redundancy substantially amplifies the footprint. Under strict datacenter power envelopes, this storage infrastructure directly competes with GPU deployment limits. We observe that datasets are already globally replicated for job scheduling, creating an opportunity to replace local multi-replica redundancy with single-local-replica storage backed by remote repair. However, eliminating local redundancy sacrifices read-time availability and reduces the read-serving capacity necessary to keep GPUs fully utilized. We present SOLO , a data orchestration system co-designed with DLRM training workloads to make single-local-replica storage practical. First, it leverages predictable data consumption orders to proactively check and repair upcoming files, preserving read-time local availability. Second, it exploits structured and skewed access patterns together with cross-job preprocessing similarity to achieve workload-aware data placement and compact intermediate reuse, preserving high-throughput data reads. We have deployed SOLO across multiple datacenters in ByteDance’s production infrastructure, serving thousands of daily jobs. SOLO reduces per-GPU storage cost by 45%–55%, saves tens of exabytes of storage and tens of megawatts of power capacity, consumes less than 1% of inter-datacenter bandwidth, and improves GPU SM activity by 1.35 × –2.41 × on I/O-bound jobs.

records.title: HybridFaaS: Efficient GPU Serverless via Hybrid Autoscaling
records.abstract: Serverless computing is widely adopted for its simplicity, autoscaling, and fine-grained billing. However, GPU-based serverless frameworks often inherit CPU-oriented designs, leading to inefficiencies in machine learning (ML) inference. Specifically, the keep-warm policy, effective on CPUs, is suboptimal on GPUs due to rigid hardware binding, and replica-based autoscaling incurs significant memory overhead and frequent model swaps, which are amplified by large machine learning models. To address these problems, we propose HybridFaaS, a hybrid autoscaling strategy that combines pipelined and tensor-parallel scaling to save memory with replica-based scaling for flexibility, reducing model swapping overhead without undue scheduling complexity. Evaluations demonstrate that HybridFaaS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art systems with 80-97% higher throughput and 99-147 × lower P99 tail latency.

records.title: System A: An Open Platform for AI-Based Bandwidth Estimation in Real-Time Communications
authors: Wenxue Cheng    Jeongyoon Eo    Zhixiong Niu    Francis Y. Yan    Rui Gao    Ze Gan
Vishak Gopal    Byung-Gon Chun    Ran Shu
records.abstract: Real-time communications (RTC), such as video conferencing and cloud gaming, rely on bandwidth estimation (BWE) to balance throughput, delay, and loss under diverse network conditions and media workloads. AI-based BWE is a promising direction beyond hand-tuned rules, but progress remains slow and fragmented because each project must rebuild the system support around the model itself: a real RTC stack for running models; environments for training, validation, and real-world evaluation; and artifacts for comparing and improving models. This paper presents OpenNetLab, an open platform for AI-based BWE in RTC. At its core, OpenNetLab provides simulator, emulator, and real-node runtimes for training, validation, and real-world evaluation. The three runtimes share AlphaRTC, which combines the WebRTC stack with a common AI-BWE interface, while runtime-specific Media and Network Engines meet the workflow’s efficiency and fidelity requirements through fast simulation, real-stack emulation, and live-Internet execution. A shared Benchmark defines reproducible cases and metrics, while Open Artifacts support independent deployment, community sharing and contributions, and continual benchmark updates. We evaluate OpenNetLab through matched-replay execution fidelity, training efficiency, and benchmark comparability. A 600-case matched-replay study shows small gaps in network and media outcomes between the OpenNetLab emulator and a WebRTC reference. A PPO training run compresses about 194 call-hours into 23 minutes of simulator time, a roughly 497 × speedup. OpenNetLab has powered the MMSys 2021 BWE Challenge and has been used in subsequent published RTC research.

records.title: ATP: Workload-Adaptive Scheduling for Goodput-Optimized Tensor-Parallel LLM Serving with PD Disaggregation
authors: Youhui Bai    Chaoyi Ruan    Jiaan Zhu    Long Zhao
records.abstract: Online LLM serving must satisfy two latency SLOs: time-to-first-token (TTFT) for responsiveness and time-between-tokens (TBT) for smooth generation. To improve resource utilization under these targets, serving systems optimize goodput, the request completion rate that satisfies both SLOs. However, modern interactive, agentic, and long-document workloads are highly skewed and time-varying, making static tensor-parallel (TP) configurations and fixed GPU splits between prefill and decoding (PD) inefficient. We present ATP, a scheduling-layer system for goodput-optimized, PD-disaggregated LLM serving. It organizes GPUs into serving instances with different fixed TP degrees, each able to serve either prefill or decoding. Over these instances, ATP formulates request-level TP selection and pool-level PD allocation as one scheduling problem and addresses it at two timescales. Its fast path routes each request’s prefill and decoding to the TP instances that best fit each stage. Its slow path adapts the PD split by changing instance roles when workload composition changes. Implemented atop vLLM, ATP achieves, on average, 2.27 × the sustainable goodput of LoongServe, 2.07 × that of DistServe, and 1.82 × that of an enhanced static baseline on real-world Mooncake traces, with mean scheduling latency below 310 μ s.

records.title: TwinCache: A Retrieval- and Reranking-Aware Caching System for Efficient RAG Serving
records.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves the factuality of large language models (LLMs) by grounding responses in external knowledge, but introduces substantial pre-generation latency. We observe that both database retrieval and neural reranking can dominate time-to-first-token (TTFT) under different serving configurations, while related queries exhibit cross-query locality in retrieved chunks and high-ranked evidence after reranking. However, existing optimizations typically target retrieval or reranking in isolation, leaving this locality underexploited across the two stages. To this end, we present TwinCache, a retrieval- and reranking-aware caching system that exploits cross-query locality to jointly accelerate both stages of RAG serving. TwinCache organizes historical queries and retrieved chunks into locality-aware cache regions and constructs a compact, high-utility candidate set for each incoming query using nearest-query evidence, historical reranking feedback, and current-query similarity. This avoids expensive database retrieval on validated cache hits while reducing the number of chunks submitted to the reranker. To further reduce pre-generation latency, TwinCache introduces priority-guided reranking, which processes high-priority chunks first, overlaps subsequent reranking with LLM chunked prefill, and stops once the leading evidence chunks stabilize. TwinCache also mitigates potential false cache hits through online validation and refreshes cache regions during low-load periods using online feedback. Across diverse serving loads, TwinCache achieves up to 2.44 × the serving throughput of a vLLM-based RAG system while maintaining response quality comparable to standard RAG.

records.title: Operating System Policies in the Wild
authors: Yushan Qin    Ananya Virmani    Sungkar Bolat    Ayushi Chaudhary    Nida Tanveer Ul Hasan    Mai Zheng    Sebastian Angel    Christopher J. Rossbach    Michael Swift
records.abstract: Operating system policies determine what should happen and when. They have a large impact on performance, and are the subject of much research. However, they are largely discussed in isolation: the single question of what thread to run next on a CPU, or what memory page to replace next. Decades of development in Linux, though, teaches us that OS policies can be both more complicated and simpler; there are also many more than commonly discussed. This paper presents a study of Linux kernel policies across multiple subsystems with the goal of better understanding what they do, how they are implemented, and how readily they can be changed. Using manual code inspection, we identify over 330 policies across the Linux memory management, scheduling, I/O, file, and power subsystems. We identify common implementation styles, such as single and multi-function decisions, inline-code and configurable parameters; common features used for decisions such as local and global state, historical context, and hardware information; common decision types such as selecting objects, identifying attributes, and changing system modes. Taken as a whole, this study presents a comprehensive picture of the diversity and common structures of Linux policies, and serves as a basis for future work in developing new ML-driven policies.

records.title: A Novel AI-Native GPU Kernel Programming Language for Autonomous Kernel Tuning
records.abstract: Autonomous LLM-driven kernel tuners have proliferated in 2025–2026, yet none produces kernels that match vendor libraries on the operators those libraries target, such as cuBLAS GEMM or cuSPARSELt sparse GEMM on Hopper GPUs. Two critical gaps explain this ceiling. First, every existing system tunes parameters within a human-supplied skeleton, so the agent cannot explore architectural alternatives such as warp specialisation, pipeline topology, or persistence mode. Second, the programming substrates these systems rely on impose compounding obstacles: large per-iteration token footprints, coupled code sites that fan a single structural change into many scattered edits, and absent compile-time feedback when a configuration is infeasible. This paper presents the first AI-native GPU kernel programming language, co-designed with AI tuning to close both gaps. In a six-DSL comparison on the same agent, H800 GPU, and iteration budget, our approach is the only programming substrate whose AI-tuned kernels consistently outperform vendor libraries, averaging 1.23 × across cuBLAS, CUTLASS, and cuSPARSELt on 95 production shapes. Trajectory analysis shows that the breakthroughs stem from structural kernel discoveries (warp specialisation, pipeline staging, TMA) rather than parameter search alone, enabled by two co-design axes. Syntax–context co-design makes structural edits practical: decoupled primitives yield the fewest code sites per feature, cutting the token footprint 1.6 × below equal-expressiveness DSLs and raising compile pass@1 to 85.7% (95.6% pass@5). Compiler–harness co-design amplifies this through compile-time pruning and structured diagnostics, sustaining 82.1% pass@1 on dynamic-shape kernels (Triton 48%) and 82.3% under moderate-capacity models where competing DSLs collapse (Triton 65.8%).

records.title: DittoCache: From CPU-Orchestrated to GPU-Centric KVCache for Efficient LLM Decoding
authors: Zewen Jin    Shannon Wang    Jiaqi Ruan
Weiguang Wang    Xia Zhu    Cheng Li
records.abstract: To cope with the growing memory capacity and bandwidth demands of autoregressive decoding, LLM frameworks offload the KVCache to host memory and retrieve only top- k KV data to GPU HBM at each step. However, existing designs remain largely CPU driven, creating coupled tradeoffs among cache management overhead, GPU cache hit ratio, miss transfer cost, retrieval granularity, accuracy, and fragmented GPU execution precluding whole-step CUDA Graphs. We present DittoCache, a GPU-centric KVCache subsystem for efficient LLM decoding. DittoCache stores offloaded KV states at token granularity to preserve top- k sparse attention semantics, while managing the on-GPU cache at KV head granularity. It reuses cached top- k KV states across adjacent decoding steps using query similarity, lightweight GPU-side metadata, and head-specific policies that improve cache hit ratio without accuracy loss. For cache misses, DittoCache devises a multi-threaded transfer engine with CPU accessible GPU buffers to efficiently move token-level KV data over PCIe, and hides miss latency with layer wise prefetching. By moving cache management and transfer control to GPU, DittoCache enables whole step CUDA Graph execution and removes CPU-induced launch bubbles. DittoCache is implemented atop SGLang and open-sourced. Evaluated on Llama3 8B and Qwen2.5 14B across Hopper GPU with 800 TFLOPS and A40 GPUs, DittoCache achieves up to 2.87 × higher offline decoding throughput on Hopper GPU and 1.59 × on A40 over three KVCache subsystems. It supports 1M and 512K token decoding on Hopper GPU and A40, respectively, where all baselines fail. For online serving with high concurrency, Hopper GPU improves decoding throughput by up to 3.94 × over full attention.

records.title: TraJudger: Structure-Guided Failure Attribution for LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Systems
records.abstract: LLM-powered multi-agent systems are increasingly deployed in production, yet diagnosing their failures remains a major operational challenge. Unlike failures in cloud architectures, which can often be diagnosed using structured diagnostic information, multi-agent system failures are embedded in unstructured natural-language interactions, cascade silently across semantic boundaries, and defy attribution due to a lack of prior domain knowledge. Existing LLM-as-a-Judge approaches treat execution trajectories holistically, misattributing cascaded failures and fabricating plausible but ungrounded explanations. To overcome the limitations of existing methods, we present TraJudger, a structure-guided failure attribution system deployed in production at a global top-tier online shopping service provider. TraJudger constructs a Hierarchical Cognitive Graph from raw trajectories to recover explicit inter-step dependencies, deploys four category-specific specialist agents for typed failure detection, and performs graph-constrained backward tracing to ground root-cause identification in verified dependency paths. On 121 production and 126 benchmark failure trajectories, TraJudger achieves a relative improvement of at least 15% and 13.3% over state-of-the-art methods at the agent and step levels. TraJudger has been deployed at \(\mathcal {C}ompany\) \(\mathcal {A}\) for over one month, reducing average time-to-attribution from 30 minutes to under one minute.

records.title: Model-as-a-Service in the Wild: Characterizing Production LLM Inference Clusters at Scale
authors: Yiyun Zheng    Lingyun Yang    Yinghao Yu
records.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference has been widely deployed in modern cloud platforms as Model-as-a-Service (MaaS), serving both online and offline applications on shared, heterogeneous GPU clusters. Recent characterization studies have examined request-level workload patterns, but cluster-wide resource patterns and system-level deployment behaviors remain largely unexplored. This missing view is critical for diagnosing production bottlenecks and for understanding whether and how existing inference techniques should be applied in real MaaS systems. In this paper, we analyze a six-month production LLM inference trace from xMaaS , a large-scale MaaS platform with over 100K GPUs. xMaaS provides a detailed system view of cluster resources and their allocation across 300K applications and 70K model variants, enabling a resource-centric analysis across cluster, application, and model levels. Our study characterizes how heterogeneous GPU resources are supplied and utilized, how application resource demand is distributed and evolves over time, and how model variants and serving modes affect resource allocation on heterogeneous hardware. Based on these observations, we further analyze deployment implications and identify open problems for production MaaS systems, which we hope will motivate future research on resource-efficient LLM inference.

records.title: D-Pingmesh: Dynamic Probing and Fault Localization for Reconfigurable Datacenter Networks
authors: Yunze Wei    Kaicheng Yang    Xiaohui Xie
Bingyang Liu    Kun Tan    Kai Chen    Yong Cui
records.abstract: Pingmesh monitors datacenter networks through periodic pings between servers. In reconfigurable datacenter networks, topology engineering (TPE) and traffic engineering (TE) make uniform server-pair probing inefficient: a pinglist wastes budget retesting common paths while missing low-probability interfaces. Frequent control-plane updates further require rapid pinglist refresh, and cause path ambiguity at control-plane boundaries for fault localization. We present D-Pingmesh, a probing and fault-localization system co-designed with the TPE/TE control plane. Its control-plane-aware generator builds task-efficient pinglists by greedily admitting probes with high interface coverage under the current TPE/TE snapshot. An incremental replay-and-repair mechanism updates pinglists across reconfigurations rather than recomputing from scratch. At control-plane boundaries, a Rho-EM localizer jointly infers per-task old/new-path mixture weights and the fault set through EM-style iteration. We evaluate D-Pingmesh on an 8-pod reconfigurable topology under dynamic TPE/TE. At a 0.99 coverage target, D-Pingmesh uses 17.7 × fewer tasks than Pingmesh and generates each pinglist about 5.1 × faster than RD-Probe. In ns-3 simulation, boundary-aware localization improves micro F1 from 0.871 to 0.953 over the deTector PLL baseline. A testbed deployment demonstrates second-scale fault localization with low host overhead. These results demonstrate that D-Pingmesh is practical for reconfigurable datacenter networks with control-plane-aware monitoring.

records.title: HeapLENS: Heap Layout Evaluation & Navigation Suite
records.abstract: We present HeapLENS, a visualization and profiling tool for spotting memory-layout anti-patterns in multithreaded C/C++ applications. It is built to investigate questions such as: Which object types routinely lie next to tree nodes? Which fields cross cache lines? How do layouts change over time? HeapLENS automatically collects allocation histories with best-effort type information and support for custom user allocators. To make histories with billions of events inspectable, it uses sampling and a novel page fingerprinting technique to cluster and visualize a small set of diverse layouts. We use HeapLENS to identify layout problems, contributing an accepted RocksDB fix, and improving concurrent data structure performance by up to 30.6%. We also give HeapLENS’s text exports to an LLM, which independently investigates layout problems and tests optimizations, improving mean throughput by 4.2% in the Valkey KV-store and approximate nearest-neighbour throughput by up to 9.8% in the HNSWLib vector database.

records.title: CAVER: Enhancing RDMA Load Balancing by Hunting Less-Congested Paths
authors: Menghao Zhang    Yuan Yang    Xiao Li    Junhao Dong
records.abstract: Load balancing (LB) is critical for reducing flow completion time (FCT) in RDMA networks where link congestion fluctuates rapidly. While many existing works have been devoted to improving LB performance in RDMA, they all select paths based on limited information, leaving a large number of available paths unexploited, which is prone to wasting the network bandwidth resources. In this paper, we aim to enhance existing works by optimizing the awareness of congestion status and propose CAVER, an RDMA-optimized LB framework. The key idea behind CAVER is to leverage ACK packets to establish a vector-protocol-like mechanism, enabling the efficient collection of real-time path congestion information and the selection of less-congested paths. We implement CAVER with NS3 and Tofino switches, and conduct simulations and real experiments. The results show that compared to state-of-the-art, CAVER improves average and 99th-percentile FCT by up to 46.0% and 32.2%, respectively.

records.title: ATLAS: Expert-Guided Sustainable Satellite Backhaul for Off-Grid Wildlife Monitoring
authors: Chi Xu    Cheng Pan    Jiangchuan Liu
records.abstract: Remote wildlife monitoring increasingly depends on high-fidelity cameras and sensors deployed far from grid power and terrestrial networks. Low Earth orbit satellite links can provide connectivity in these settings, but their high power draw and variable bandwidth, combined with intermittent on-site solar harvesting, make continuous backhaul infeasible. Current systems therefore filter at the edge, with motion triggers that waste limited energy and bandwidth on environmental artifacts, or fixed vision models that cannot follow evolving expert objectives. We present ATLAS , an expert-guided edge-to-cloud system that treats satellite backhaul as a scarce resource for off-grid wildlife monitoring. ATLAS uses foundation models to compile natural-language expert intent into semantic scoring logic, combines semantic relevance with environmental and energy state, and uses a constrained reinforcement-learning scheduler to decide which clips to upload and when. As a representative case study, we deployed ATLAS for over six months across 18 off-grid salmon-monitoring river sites. ATLAS achieves a mean clip-selection accuracy of \(87.4\%\) , exceeding mean baseline accuracy by 26.4 percentage points, while maintaining near-continuous operation through low-solar periods in which baselines incur 16.0% downtime.

records.title: Instrumentation Optimization for Practical Dynamic Race Detection
records.abstract: Dynamic data race detectors are successful at flagging concurrency bugs, but their high runtime overhead limits adoption. This overhead stems primarily from pervasive instrumentation of memory accesses – a significant fraction of which is for safe accesses. We address this inefficiency through a compiler-integrated approach that identifies safe accesses using static analysis and eliminates instrumentation for these. We strike a careful balance between analysis precision and cost, to ensure applicability to real-world applications. We show that our optimizations never cause ThreadSanitizer to miss races it would otherwise detect. We further observe that many checks are redundant: They only flag a race if a preceding check has already flagged an equivalent race for the same memory location. We show that, when reporting one representative per class is sufficient, even more instrumentation can be eliminated. Lastly, we introduce a dynamic technique that skips instrumentation when there is only one thread at runtime, even when this could not be determined statically. We integrate these static analyses and program transformations into the ThreadSanitizer race detector based on LLVM. Our experiments on a diverse suite of real-world applications, including Memcached, Redis, SQLite, MySQL, and Chromium, demonstrate that our optimizations reduce the number of instrumentation calls at runtime by up to 91% and yield application-level speedups of up to 1.91 ×, a geometric-mean Chromium speedup of 1.25 × on Blink and 1.14 × on Speedometer 3.0, and peak speedups reaching 2.28 × on Memcached with two server threads. Our optimizations are in the process of being upstreamed into ThreadSanitizer.

records.title: SymRDMA: Enabling In-Situ Remote Virtual Memory Sharing
authors: Huijun Shen    Bojie Li    Haixin Pang    Peihao Huang    Xingtong Lin
records.abstract: Data-intensive distributed applications, including in-memory analytics, distributed storage, and graph systems, increasingly demand in-situ remote virtual memory sharing, which refers to application-managed virtual memory (typically unpinned and dynamically changing) that remote peers access directly (e.g., the live JVM heap used by Spark). Realizing this on RDMA forces a dilemma: either copy into small pinned buffers, sacrificing zero-copy, or pin the entire heap—which disables OS elasticity and, for managed runtimes, is often architecturally impossible. Hardware-based On-Demand Paging (ODP) bridges the gap but suffers throughput collapse. This paper presents SymRDMA, the first system to enable high-performance in-situ remote virtual memory sharing on commodity RDMA hardware, transparently and with no hardware modifications. SymRDMA handles page faults optimistically via three mechanisms: (1) Optimistic Fault Suppression , using a hardware-enforced Sentinel Page to trap faults without breaking connections; (2) lightweight Remote Seqlocks to detect host-side changes without blocking the OS; and (3) Server-Initiated Repair , converting faults into targeted reverse-RDMA operations that avoid head-of-line blocking and timeouts. As a user-space library compatible with unmodified applications and hardware, SymRDMA achieves 11–14 × lower graph-traversal latency than gRPC and 5–7 × than ODP, runs Spark 1.5–1.7 × faster than production, and expands storage capacity 5 × with only 9% latency increase (vs. 45% for copying, 6 × for ODP).

records.title: JANUS: Practical Load Balancing for Confidential Cloud Services
records.abstract: Confidential computing enables a cloud service to prove, by remote attestation, that it runs inside a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE). Recent work has bound this attestation to Transport Layer Security (TLS) so that a client can verify TEEs via the TLS channel, but these designs assume a client talking to a single specific attested server. Realistic cloud services, however, are not run on single servers: they are load-balanced, structured as a frontend fronting an elastic pool of backend servers. Extending current attested-TLS designs onto this pool is problematic, forcing either custom client logic, a Certificate Authority (CA) certificate issuance per backend server, or a fresh attestation on every connection. We present Janus , a practical load-balancing architecture for confidential cloud services. Specifically, a small attested frontend, running inside a TEE, holds the only client-facing TLS identity: it obtains a CA-issued X.509 certificate that carries its attestation evidence in a certificate extension. The frontend then admits backend servers, attesting each and signing its public key using a short-lived RFC-9345 Delegated Credential so that every backend serves client traffic under the frontend’s single attested identity. This also allows each backend to be attested only once at admission rather than per client connection. Janus piggybacks on what the TLS ecosystem has deployed or is developing — X.509 certificate extensions, ACME certificate issuance, and Delegated Credentials — so it complies with the current networking practices and trends, and changes nothing in the TLS protocol. It supports standard load-balancing modes (i.e., proxy and redirection). Our evaluation shows that the marginal connection-establishment cost of Janus is as low as 4 ms (in proxy mode) and 12 ms (in redirection mode), compared with vanilla TLS.

records.title: Zswap Boost: Accelerating Transparent Memory Compression in the Cloud
authors: Zheng Liu    Teng Ma    Chengkun Wei    Ning Zhang    Xingyu Liu    Gang Deng    Shangming Cai    Wenzhi Chen
records.abstract: Memory is one of the most expensive and underutilized resources in cloud datacenters. Transparent memory compression reclaims overcommitted memory without additional hardware or application changes. Yet our production deployment of Linux zswap reveals substantial overhead for latency-sensitive workloads. Although compressed pages remain in memory, zswap retains disk-oriented swap indexing, red-black-tree lookup, swap-cache management, and slot allocation. Consequently, roughly 40% of swap-in critical-path CPU cycles are spent on bookkeeping rather than decompression. To eliminate this disk-centric tax, we present Zswap Boost, which encodes the compressed-page metadata location in the page-table entry. It reduces zswap’s three-level lookup to two and removes swap-slot, red-black-tree, and swap-cache operations from the critical path. We also integrate Intel IAA using batched compression and asynchronous decompression. Zswap Boost is implemented in our commercial Linux distribution and has run in production for nearly two years. In controlled experiments, Zswap Boost reduces swap-in latency from 6.6 ∼ 19.9 μs to 2.5 ∼ 4.3 μs , cuts Flink kernel-mode CPU time from 54.3% to 19.0%, and saves 12.5% of memory at a 2.13% performance cost. It also reduces Redis P99 latency by up to 18.5% compared with vanilla zswap. In our Flink cluster, the broader memory-overcommit pipeline enabled 130 physical machines to be retired.

records.title: NosRacer: Dynamic Detection of Race Conditions in On-Device Network Operating Systems
records.abstract: Commercial on-device network operating systems (NOSes) run the complex control planes of production routers and switches, where configuration update tasks are executed by multiple loosely coupled components through asynchronous message passing. Such executions are prone to race conditions: the same ordered input commands may produce different outcomes when messages are delivered in different orders. The race conditions are difficult to expose because they often manifest only as subtle, delayed malfunctions. Existing static analysis techniques lack scalability and precision for large-scale industrial NOSes, while dynamic ones incur substantial system-execution cost when attempting to cover the space of asynchronous message interleavings. To address the challenges above, we present NosRacer , a dynamic analysis framework for race condition detection in industrial-grade on-device NOSes. NosRacer uses a two-phase design. The concentration phase reduces analysis scope by leveraging the locality of configuration update tasks. Race condition detection is then limited to a small subset of involved components and crucial state variables, thereby reducing the detection cost. The perturbation phase proactively perturbs message asynchrony to increase the likelihood of executions with race-condition-exposing message interleavings. It keeps perturbation practical by grouping compatible perturbations for parallel execution and adaptively strengthening perturbations. We implement NosRacer in a commercial, actively developed NOS. NosRacer is integrated into the existing testing factory and used to detect race conditions in 5 key control-plane components. NosRacer achieves 66% precision and detects 21 race conditions confirmed by developers as severe bugs, while keeping the detection overhead below 10%.

records.title: Lean: Saving OSS Network Cost by Application-Infrastructure Coordination
authors: Jiashi Lu    Xue Li    Qingchao Luo
records.abstract: Network is the single largest line item in a hyperscale Object Storage Service (OSS), consuming roughly 40% of an annual infrastructure bill measured in hundreds of millions of dollars. Two tiers dominate: the access network, where client traffic is locked into expensive in-region EdgePoPs despite 2–5 × cheaper off-region bandwidth being widely available; and the intra-region network, where 3AZ replication amplifies every write into massive cross-AZ traffic that accounts for a substantial share of the network bill. We present Lean, a dedicated system that breaks through this barrier via application-infrastructure co-design, using SRv6 as a single unifying primitive to enable three capabilities: lightweight ingress units deployable at any EdgePoP, arbitrary traffic steering, and physical isolation of OSS traffic. In production for 4 years serving O (1 B ) objects and O (10 K ) enterprise customers, Lean has cut the OSS network bill by 55.6%, saving hundreds of millions of dollars annually.

records.title: FlashCodec: Unleash All Decoding Resources for Low-Latency Video Decoding in MLLM Inference
records.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly support video understanding workloads, where video decoding constitutes a substantial portion of end-to-end inference latency, as raw video streams must be decoded into pixel frames before model processing. However, existing frameworks fail to effectively leverage abundant decoding resources (e.g., CPUs and NVDECs ) to minimize per-video decoding latency while maintaining high throughput. As a result, video decoding becomes a dominant contributor to the Time-To-First-Token (TTFT). This inefficiency arises from inter-frame dependency constraints in video decoding, device-level heterogeneity between CPU and GPU, and intrinsic limitations of decoding resources themselves, along with GPU resource contention with co-located MLLM inference, collectively limiting effective resource utilization. In this paper, we present FlashCodec, a video decoding framework designed to effectively utilize heterogeneous decoding resources for low-latency, high-throughput video decoding. FlashCodec introduces: (1) a dependency-isolated GOP-level scheduling scheme that enables parallelism without redundant decoding; (2) a runtime adaptive scheduler that dynamically assigns GOPs to heterogeneous decoders without pre-allocation, guided by device characteristics to maximize utilization; and (3) an SM-light decoding pipeline that minimizes reliance on GPU SMs, reducing interference under co-located inference. Together, these techniques enable efficient and low-latency video decoding for latency-critical online MLLM inference. Experiments across a wide range of codecs and GPU servers show that FlashCodec achieves 6.8–25.7 × decoding speedup over out-of-the-box implementations with over 90% peak efficiency, surpasses static chunking parallelization strategies 2.7-7.0 × in latency and 2.6-9.8 × in throughput, incurs minimal overhead when co-located with MLLM services, and enables up to 7.1 × stricter TTFT SLOs in end-to-end inference.

records.title: A^2: Characterizing and Mitigating Imbalanced Reclaim in MGLRU via Active Aging at Production Scale
authors: Ligeng Chen    Yinggang Guo    Hao Wu    Lu Liu
Jun Xiao    Borui Li    Feng Lyu
records.abstract: Multi-generational LRU (MGLRU) has been adopted by some major smartphone manufacturers to replace the dual-list LRU, delivering lower kswapd CPU consumption, fewer low-memory kills, and reduced rendering latency under memory pressure. However, our production deployment revealed a regression: cold anonymous pages are shielded from reclaim by MGLRU’s aging gate, forcing hot file pages to be evicted first; swappiness, the canonical parameter for balancing anonymous and file reclaim, is thereby bypassed. The root cause is an asymmetry: anonymous pages must age through multiple generations before becoming reclaimable, yet at default priority, aging is deferred; file pages are reclaimed from the oldest generation immediately. We propose an Active Aging mechanism, \(\mathtt {A^2}\) , which decouples aging from reclaim by triggering it when pages turn cold. On Android, the foreground-to-background transition provides this moment: userspace invokes the kernel’s existing page-table scan, opening the aging gate before reclaim runs. The approach is not Android-specific; servers running MGLRU can apply the same aging primitive via a BPF hook to correct the generational imbalance. \(\mathtt {A^2}\) deployed across 300 users over 30K device-hours, \(\mathtt {A^2}\) improves Android keep-alive by 15.4%, and input method editor (IME) dismiss latency by 47.2%. In server workload measurements, it improves fio random-read bandwidth by 31.83%. Code and benchmark specifications are available at https://github.com/ccfeiker/mglru-active-aging .

records.title: Medivh: Harnessing Compatible and Accurate Sketch-based Network Measurement with Sparsity-based Virtualization
authors: Xiang Chen    Feng Zhu    Hongmin Tan
records.abstract: Sketches build their data structures in data plane switches to perform approximate measurements towards high-speed traffic. However, switch resources constraints create an intractable trade-off between the compatibility with network functions and high accuracy. Allocating enough resources to sketches affects concurrent network functions and results in loss of compatibility. In contrast, without enough resources, sketches suffer from accuracy loss. We propose Medivh, a framework that achieves both compatibility and high accuracy in sketch-based network measurement. For compatibility, Medivh uses residual switch resources to place sketches, avoiding affecting concurrent network functions. For high accuracy, it leverages the sparsity of sketch data, i.e., only a few values are non-zero due to traffic skewness, to implement a sketchlet hypervisor. This hypervisor virtualizes sketch rows, i.e., sketchlets, by mapping multiple virtual sketchlets to a shared physical hash table that stores only non-zero values. Hence, every sketch can work with enough resources and provide high accuracy. We evaluate Medivh with various sketches, diverse production workloads and applications. (1) In our testbed comprising 32 × 400 Gbps Tofino2 switches, Medivh improves accuracy by 24.4%–88.7% under strict compatibility. (2) In production use cases, it boosts sketch placement, supports distributed attack detection, and handles runtime dynamics.

records.title: Joseph: Hypervisor–RDMA Co-Design for Kernel-Bypass Remote MicroVM SnapStart
authors: Kanye Ye Wang    Dazhao Cheng    Xiaobo Zhou
records.abstract: Modern serverless platforms such as AWS Lambda increasingly use MicroVM SnapStart to pair lightweight isolation with fast startup. However, restoring snapshots from remote disaggregated memory to local DRAM induces layered copies and fault-driven stalls along the NIC → kernel → VMM → guest datapath, inflating latency and limiting scalability under high concurrency. We present Joseph, a hypervisor–RDMA co-designed system that treats the hypervisor as a first-class RDMA endpoint for fast remote MicroVM SnapStart. Joseph’s key principle is a network-to-guest placement contract: each RDMA read targets the guest frame of the faulting page, and the EPT mapping is installed only after the corresponding RDMA completion. This couples network transfer with guest-memory visibility in a single VMM/RNIC operation. Joseph builds a kernel-bypass RNIC → guest data path to place snapshot data directly into guest pages, bypassing kernel buffers and coalescing remote page fetches to amortize latency. By integrating RNIC-driven data placement into the hypervisor’s memory path, Joseph (i) enables direct access to remote snapshot pages, (ii) pipelines scatter–gather page fetches within the VMM pager, and (iii) uses RNIC-offloaded guest-memory fetch for in-situ page mapping, enabling zero-copy restoration and reducing CPU contention. Implemented on Firecracker/KVM, Joseph achieves up to 77% (87%) lower SnapStart latency, 2 × (3 ×) higher concurrency, and 81% (56%) higher memory efficiency under high-concurrency workloads, compared to FaaSnap (TrEnv).

records.title: Octopus: Unlocking SSD Parallelism for Sparse KV Cache Retrieval
records.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache has become the dominant contributor to memory consumption in large language model (LLM) inference. Although offloading KVCache from GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to CPU DRAM alleviates device memory pressure, DRAM remains capacity-limited and costly for large, persistent workloads. Solid-state drives (SSDs) provide a cost-effective alternative, but naive SSD-based paging is fundamentally bandwidth-bound due to limited PCIe throughput and per-device bandwidth constraints. In this paper, we observe that KVCache activations in real-world workloads exhibit strong and stable correlations. We term this phenomenon KVCache Co-Activation , where accessing a KV entry is often accompanied by a recurring set of other KV entries. Leveraging this property, we present Octopus , an SSD-based KVCache offloading system that converts bandwidth-bound single-device access into parallel I/O across multiple SSDs. Specifically, Octopus clusters co-activated KV entries offline and distributes the resulting clusters across SSDs using graph-based placement with selective replication to maximize parallel bandwidth. At runtime, Octopus performs load-balanced cluster retrieval and dynamically adapts clustering and caching decisions to sustain high bandwidth utilization under evolving access patterns. Evaluations show that Octopus improves serving throughput by 1.42 × and effective bandwidth utilization by 2.67 ×. The code is available at https://github.com/omnimind-ai/Octopus.

records.title: MoE-Lego: A Plane-Grained System for Dynamic-Precision MoE Offloading
authors: Cheng Xu    Jiacheng Liu    Chao Li
records.abstract: Multi-precision inference balances serving efficiency and model quality for large MoE LLMs under limited memory. However, changing expert precision at runtime exposes a fundamental tradeoff in existing systems: they either waste GPU memory by storing multiple precision replicas, or incur high I/O overhead by reloading whole expert tensors. Thus, achieving both dynamic precision and efficient execution remains an open challenge. We present MoE-Lego, an end-to-end MoE inference system that uses bitplane representation as the substrate for dynamic multi-precision execution. MoE-Lego first constructs a single nested bitplane artifact with routing-aligned calibration, so all supported precisions share the same base planes. Its runtime scheduler changes precision by moving, retaining, and demoting only the required bitplanes, making the I/O cost approximately proportional to the bit-width delta instead of the full expert size. Its GPU executor treats target precision as an execution dimension: it builds precision buckets for routed FFN work and computes each bucket with grouped bitplane kernels, avoiding fragmented per-expert computation. Across Qwen1.5-MoE, Qwen3-MoE, and Phi-3.5-MoE on A100 and RTX 4090, MoE-Lego achieves geometric-mean speedups of 3.72 × for prefill and 2.83 × for decode over the baselines, while preserving near-16-bit model quality. An additional evaluation on Jetson Orin demonstrates its applicability to SSD-backed expert offloading.

records.title: Chorus: GPU–CPU Cooperative LLM Serving for Length-Skewed Decode
authors: Sheng Yao    Ruichuan Chen    Binhang Yuan
records.abstract: Online LLM serving is increasingly constrained by GPU memory capacity during decode. In length-skewed workloads, a small fraction of long requests keeps large key-value (KV) caches resident across many decode steps, exhausting GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM), throttling admission, and reducing goodput for the short-request majority. At the same time, GPU servers provision substantial CPU and DRAM resources, and recent Intel CPUs add Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) for matrix-heavy kernels. The challenge is to use these host resources without placing CPU work on the per-token GPU critical path. We present Chorus , a GPU–CPU cooperative serving system that uses AMX-equipped CPUs as a second decode lane for long requests with persistent KV state. Chorus keeps prefill and short-request decode on GPUs, offloads selected long-request decode once to distributed AMX CPU groups, and releases the corresponding GPU KV pages so the GPU lane can admit more short requests. To satisfy online service level objectives (SLOs), Chorus combines pressure-aware offload admission, tensor-parallel AMX decode that aggregates CPU compute and memory bandwidth, and AMX kernels specialized for small, mixed-length decode batches. Across popular LLMs and production-derived workloads, Chorus achieves the highest SLO-attaining goodput among baselines, improving peak goodput over SGLang by up to 1.26 ×. At the same offered load, Chorus delivers 1.3–11.4 × SGLang’s goodput when GPU-only serving enters time-to-first-token (TTFT) collapse, and improves over CPU-offload baselines by up to 4.3 ×.

records.title: InfiniLoRA: Disaggregated Multi-LoRA Serving for Large Language Models
authors: Letian Ruan    Zilin Xu    Yuchen Li    Xinyu Chen  )  Bingsheng He    Jingwen Leng
records.abstract: LoRA enables efficient customization of LLMs and is widely used in multi-tenant and multi-task serving. However, emerging model architectures such as MoE significantly increase LoRA memory cost, making existing coupled LoRA serving designs poorly scalable and prone to tail-latency inflation. We present InfiniLoRA, a disaggregated LoRA serving system that decouples LoRA execution from base-model inference. InfiniLoRA introduces a shared LoRA Server with parallelism-aware execution, SLO-driven provisioning, and critical-path optimizations, including GPU-initiated communication and hardware-specialized LoRA kernels. Experiments show that InfiniLoRA can achieve an average 3.05 × increase in serviceable request rate under strict latency SLOs, and improves the percentage of LoRA adapters satisfying the SLO requirement by 53.1%.

records.title: Dasheng: LLM-powered Reliability Engineering Assistant for Cloud Overlay Networks
authors: Yining Qi    Chongrong Fang    Xiaoqing Sun    Tong Wu    Jiaxiang Chen    Xiaobo Xue    Shize Zhang    Xiaonan Shi
records.abstract: Amid mounting incidents of network failures, cloud service providers are placing increasing emphasis on reliability engineering. Leveraging their capabilities in text understanding and reasoning, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been integrated to assist conventional cloud network reliability tools. However, deploying an LLM-powered reliability engineering assistant to cloud overlay networks is significantly challenging due to the scale, complexity, and intricate couplings of cloud overlay network components. In this work, we present Dasheng, an LLM-powered reliability engineering assistant for cloud overlay networks. Dasheng extends the standard assistant paradigm with an iterative, multi-step tool interaction mechanism to fit the characteristics of cloud overlay networks. Dasheng has been deployed on a production cloud for two years. To date, it has been used by 1,450 engineers for approximately 70k invocations. Most Dasheng invocations complete within 3-100 seconds, and reduce case resolution time by up to 97%. In 92% of evaluated cases, Dasheng produces useful outputs that materially assist engineers.

records.title: BPFFoundary: Scalable and Practical Multi eBPF Program Composition and Testing at Meta.
records.abstract: At scale, many eBPF programs developed by different teams must coexist on the same hosts (i.e., multi-tenancy) and share maps, across a fleet running varying kernel versions. Unfortunately, the interactions among these programs, their shared maps, and the kernel versions they run on can lead to failures and production incidents. More importantly, the kernel verifier does not check these interactions: they fall outside the notion of safety it enforces. We present BPFFoundary, a framework developed at Meta to provide two forms of safety: compositional safety, where BPFWeaver detects and arbitrates conflicts among programs and their shared maps, and emergent safety, where eBPF-CICD proactively exposes programs to a broad range of kernel versions, hardware, application traffic and edge cases to detect failures. Although these mechanisms provide fundamentally different forms of safety, managing eBPF programs at our scale requires both and so we developed BPFFoundary to address both. We have evaluated BPFFoundary across millions of hosts, and it is used by multiple teams. BPFWeaver has prevented 1,227 issues in a recent 30-day window, and eBPF-CICD has detected and prevented failures in 9.8–12.4% of eBPF releases in our host-networking pipelines.

records.title: Dynamic Analysis of Unsafe Rust: Behaviors and Benchmarks
authors: Dylan O'Neill    Prince Noah Johnson    Zhixiao Zhang
records.abstract: Rust permits the use of unsafe code, which can violate both memory safety and concurrency safety. Prior work investigates unsafe code in Rust projects and provides insights into what, how, and why it is used. However, these studies provide only static metrics about unsafe code, while lacking an understanding of its dynamic behaviors at execution time. In parallel, many security mechanisms have been proposed to mitigate unsafe code in Rust. But the evaluations of these tools are suboptimal due to the lack of a benchmark suite that emphasizes unsafe code. In this paper, we present the first empirical study of the runtime behavior of unsafe code in real-world Rust projects. We develop a dynamic analysis framework that programmers can use to answer key questions about unsafe code at execution time. Moreover, using the dynamic analysis framework, we curate the first benchmark suite specifically designed for evaluating the performance and memory overhead of security defenses against unsafe code in Rust.

records.title: RunaSan: A Rust-Native Sanitizer for Precise and Context-Sensitive Sanitization
records.abstract: Rust guarantees memory safety by design and is increasingly used in systems software, yet the use of unsafe Rust can still introduce memory bugs. For this reason, prior works have leveraged sanitizers to detect memory errors stemming from unsafe Rust code. The shared objective is to instrument Rust programs selectively such that only the unsafe portions of code and their propagation are validated. However, previous approaches that retrofit the existing static analysis and sanitizer implementations are limited. They propagate unsafety over LLVM IR, where precision loss occurs due to the erased Rust semantics, and employ a context-insensitive pointer analysis since a context-sensitive one incurs high computational complexity. Moreover, the unsafety propagation is performed solely using static analysis, and thus cannot eliminate redundant checks in safe runtime contexts. We present RunaSan , a Rust-native analysis and instrumentation framework for sanitization of Rust: a context-sensitive sanitizer that keeps its entire analysis on Rust MIR to take advantage of Rust language semantics and evade redundant checks at runtime in safe contexts. RunaSan ’s MIR-native unsafety analysis uses Rust semantics for improved precision. A context-sensitive MIR pointer analysis is made feasible through summarization of the Rust standard library. Also, its tagged-pointer scheme allows a pointer’s safety to be recognized by sanitizer checks such that unnecessary checks can be evaded at runtime. RunaSan runs 3.25 × faster than AddressSanitizer (ASan) while detecting the same memory safety bugs on a corpus of reproduced bugs.

records.title: REFlash: Reducing Total Endurance Cost in Flash-Based Tiering via Cross-Tier Write Balancing
records.abstract: QLC SSDs offer high density and low cost per byte, but their limited write endurance remains a critical barrier to widespread deployment. Flash-based tiering mitigates this limitation by placing a higher-endurance SSD as a buffer tier in front of a QLC capacity tier. However, existing schemes fail to jointly optimize write-induced wear across tiers: in-place-update schemes incur high device-level write amplification, while log-structured schemes leave the trade-off between buffer-tier garbage collection (GC) and capacity-tier flush writes unoptimized. This paper presents REFlash, a cost-aware log-structured buffering scheme for SSD-SSD tiered storage. REFlash introduces Total Endurance Cost (TEC) , a unified metric that captures the asymmetric replacement cost across the buffer and capacity tiers, and uses it to dynamically choose between host-level GC and flush during segment reclamation. REFlash further reduces GC overhead by exploiting the bounded lifetime of buffered data. Implemented as a block device driver on an FDP-enabled TLC SSD and a QLC SSD, REFlash reduces TEC by up to 31% over existing log-structured tiering schemes while maintaining write throughput comparable to the best-performing baseline.

records.title: DAG-KV: DAG-Guided KV Propagation for Structure-Aware Knowledge Reuse
records.abstract: Knowledge-augmented LLM serving systems often repeatedly encode retrieved external knowledge, increasing time-to-first-token (TTFT) and wasting computation across requests. Existing reuse-oriented systems reduce this overhead by caching context-derived states, but adapting these states to new queries requires additional recomputation or latent-state routing. Recent knowledge-unit-level reuse methods store fine-grained knowledge units as independently reusable KV tokens, but treat related units as isolated memory items, weakening the dependencies needed for multi-hop reasoning. DAG-KV addresses this limitation by decoupling reusable knowledge content from query-specific knowledge structure. It stores each knowledge unit as an independently reusable KV token, while recovering a compact query-specific DAG over selected tokens at serving time. This DAG guides lightweight attention propagation among KV tokens, allowing related knowledge units to interact along structured reasoning paths without being serialized into the prompt or re-encoded as a joint context. We implement DAG-KV as an end-to-end prototype by adding a localized attention-level propagation step over selected KV tokens in decoder-only LLMs. Across six knowledge-intensive QA datasets, DAG-KV improves the average LLM-Judge score of independent KV-token reuse from 0.36 to 0.55 under Qwen3-4B-Instruct, and approaches the evaluated graph-retrieval RAG baseline with Qwen3-14B-Instruct, while achieving a 9.6 × average TTFT speedup over evaluated latent-memory reuse baseline under our single-request evaluation.

records.title: Flitter: Exploiting Voltage Glitches and Frequency Jitter to Create Cross-core Covert Channels on Modern CPUs
authors: Yucheng Ji    Chang Liu    Trevor E. Carlson    Dongsheng Wang
records.abstract: Software-based analog attacks that exploit power, frequency or other analog signals to leak secrets have emerged as a significant threat to CPU security, but existing methods often depend on scalable and stable frequencies or specific CPU states, making implementation challenging. This paper explores the impact of voltage glitches on CPU frequency, showing that glitches on certain cores can cause timing instability in others. Building on this observation, we propose Flitter, the first cross-core covert channel based on timing variance, which does not rely on specific CPU states or scalable frequency. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Flitter on 8 Intel CPUs and 4 AMD CPUs, achieving a transmission rate of 125 bps with an error rate of 0.83%. We further demonstrate its practicality in real-world scenarios, including virtual machines, Intel SGX, and AMD SEV.

records.title: FLASH: Fault-Led, Attested, Secure Hybrid-Key Checkpoint for Confidential GPU
authors: Jonghyun Lee    Taewoon Kang    Pratheek B    Yongqin Wang    Rachit Rajat    Mengyuan Li    Gunjae Koo    Daniel Wong    Murali Annavaram
records.abstract: GPU Confidential Computing (CC) enables secure LLM inference in production, combining a CPU TEE with NVIDIA’s GPU TEE to protect models and user data from a malicious cloud operator. As long-running LLMs are failure-prone, traditional cloud systems rely on backups, and live migration using checkpoint and restore to deal with failures. In particular, during LLM serving, GPUs build up a massive key-value (KV) cache that accelerates the decode process. But when using GPU CC, these recovery methods fail, as the GPU’s memory state, such as the KV cache, can’t be efficiently checkpointed. Checkpointing GPU memory requires encrypting the GPU data and transmitting to the CPU over the PCIe, which the CPU then decrypts using its shared key with the GPU. This encryption and decryption sequence over the PCIe leads to a 5.5 × bandwidth penalty. The decrypted data is then re-encrypted with a new set of keys shared by the CPU and a destination server which adds overhead to the already-long checkpoint latency. LLM serving is stalled for the entire duration of checkpointing; a secure full-dump of an 80 GB H100 memory takes roughly 11 s. Alternatively, tracking write operations and selectively checkpointing these written pages is a preferable path, as only a small fraction of the KV cache is updated after each decode round. Current GPUs, however, lack the ability to track dirty pages. We present FLASH , a checkpoint/recovery (C/R) system for GPU CC that is both secure (providing confidentiality, integrity, and freshness against a malicious operator) and low latency. FLASH eliminates needless decryption of GPU state during checkpoint creation. FLASH preserves the GPU-encrypted HBM data as is without decryption. The CPU then creates a heterogeneous encryption package: (1) the CPU’s own memory state and the key used to encrypt the GPU CC is encrypted into a single bundle using keys shared by the CPU and a destination server that stores the checkpoint. (2) The GPU-encrypted HBM data is preserved as a second bundle within this heterogeneous package. This approach eliminates redundant decrypt-then-reencrypt overheads for GPU CC state. FLASH also presents a novel approach to track dirty pages to enable incremental checkpointing. FLASH enhances the GPU’s unified virtual memory (UVM) driver to downgrade any GPU page that is already checkpointed to a read-only page. It then uses the write fault mechanism to track modified pages at a 2 MB granularity. This approach requires no source code modifications to the LLM code base. Lastly, FLASH classifies never-written allocations, such as model weights, and removes them from repeated checkpoint copies while continuing to track them for correctness. On an H100 with Intel TDX running vLLM, FLASH reduces checkpoint stall latency up to 9.4 × over state-of-the-art GPU C/R systems.

records.title: BPF-Ext: Safely Extending the eBPF Compilation Pipeline with Native Operations
authors: Yusheng Zheng    Zhengjie Ji    weichen tao    Hao Sun    Wei Zhang    Dan Williams    Andi Quinn
records.abstract: eBPF safely extends OS kernels in production by verifying bytecode before execution, and many of its uses are performance critical. However, its design favors safety over speed: the instruction set is designed to be verifiable, and the kernel just-in-time compiler (JIT) stays simple to remain trustworthy, translating one opcode at a time. As a result, eBPF takes up to twice as long to run as native code, and the clearest losses come from hardware idioms, operations that CPUs execute as a single instruction but eBPF lacks. Current approaches like optimizing the bytecode cannot emit these instructions, and adding them to the eBPF instruction set requires changing the compiler, the verifier, and the JIT for each architecture. Optimizing in the JIT instead enlarges the trusted computing base (TCB). We present BPF-Ext, an extension interface that lets kernel modules introduce new operations, such as native instructions, without further kernel patches or verifier changes. Our key insight is that a new operation can be verified through an equivalent vanilla eBPF form, while the CPU runs its native code. The verifier checks the eBPF form but never sees the native code, so the code that generates it is the only code each operation adds to the TCB. We prove in Lean 4 that it matches its eBPF form. Using BPF-Ext, we build Kinsn, seven hardware-idiom operations such as rotate and conditional select. On x86-64 and ARM64, Kinsn speeds up microbenchmarks by 24% and 22% and production applications by up to 12%. The same interface also supports replacing whole programs with native code, speeding up Cilium by 19% at the cost of a larger TCB.

records.title: MBCheck: Practical Static Analysis Framework for Detecting Memory Ordering Violations under WMM
records.abstract: Memory-ordering violations in lock-free kernel code, where threads share data without locks, are a high-impact source of faults that are hard to detect and debug. On architectures with a weak memory model (WMM), such as AArch64 and RISC-V, a missing release, a misplaced fence, or an ordinary load in place of an acquire can allow other CPUs to observe partially constructed memory objects. The Linux Kernel Memory Model (LKMM), evaluated with the herd7 tool, is the definitive reference for deciding whether such an outcome is allowed. However, herd7 only decides this for a small multi-threaded program, a litmus test , that a developer writes by hand. As a result, the model covers only a fraction of the millions of cross-function interactions in the kernel. MBCheck addresses this gap. It is an extensible static analysis framework that transforms a complete kernel build into a collection of automatically synthesized litmus tests and evaluates them with herd7 . MBCheck reduces each function to the shared accesses around its memory-ordering instructions, discards function pairs that cannot run concurrently, and synthesizes a litmus test for every remaining pair, together with the outcome that a missing ordering would allow. A runtime verifier checks that each litmus test is faithful to the kernel code. For a complete kernel build, MBCheck synthesizes and evaluates about 30,000 litmus tests in under an hour. On Linux v7.3-rc4, we report 47 memory-ordering violations and have submitted 41 patches to the kernel maintainers. Five of the violations have been confirmed so far, and two fixes have been accepted.

records.title: RS-Infer: A Fast and Secure LLM Inference System for Mobile Devices with Recallable Resource Isolation
records.abstract: The adoption of device-side Large Language Models (LLMs) has grown rapidly, offering stronger privacy and higher availability than their cloud-side counterparts. Attackers may compromise the OS kernel to steal valuable model weights and user data. ARM TrustZone is the de facto hardware-based isolation technology on mobile devices, used to protect sensitive applications from a compromised OS. However, protecting LLM inference with TrustZone incurs significant overhead for both the secure inference and the normal applications, due to two challenges: the inflexible resource isolation and the inefficient secure resource management. To address these challenges, this paper presents RS-Infer, a fast and secure LLM inference system for mobile devices. The key idea is to decouple the access permission from the management permission of secure resources, so that the normal-world OS cannot access them but can still manage them as usual. First, RS-Infer introduces a Recallable Resource Isolation mechanism to construct Recallable Secure Memory (RS-Memory) and a Recallable Secure NPU (RS-NPU). They can only be accessed by the secure world, but can be efficiently allocated and reclaimed by the normal-world OS. Based on them, RS-Infer further introduces the RS-Infer Framework to run secure LLM inference in the secure world. It cooperates with the normal-world OS to manage secure memory. We evaluate an RS-Infer prototype against a TrustZone-based Strawman and its optimized variant. RS-Infer achieves average TTFT speedups of 8.00 × and 2.19 × , respectively, and average response latency speedups of 14.15 × and 2.94 × for multi-model agent workflows.

records.title: KVLite: Efficient LLM Agent Scheduling via Head-Aware KV Sharing
records.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being applied in agentic applications through complex prompting structures, including fixed system prompts and the reuse of historical messages. However, existing service systems suffer from severe inefficiency due to redundant computation caused by shared text segments. Existing KV reuse strategies often fall short due to either stringent application conditions or accuracy degradation resulting from the neglect of the dynamic nature of attention distributions. We propose KVLite, a service framework based on KV sharing for agentic applications. At the algorithm level, KVLite identifies the critical heads in each layer, recomputes the KV cache for these heads to achieve a balance between high accuracy and low recomputation overhead. At the system level, KVLite identifies and shortens the critical path in agentic workflows based on KV sharing. Experimental evaluations across multiple LLM and agent benchmarks show that KVLite can significantly outperform state-of-the-art baselines, achieving a 2.1 × –3.9 × speedup in prefill latency and 2.3 × to 4.6 × improvement in throughput, with negligible accuracy loss compared to the recomputation baseline.
