records.title: Fluid-Structure Interaction Simulation of Nuclear Reactors with Ultra-Large-Scale Meshes on GPU Clusters
records.abstract: To overcome mapping bottlenecks and resource underutilization in large-scale nuclear reactor fluid-structure interaction simulations on heterogeneous supercomputers, we propose a GPU-accelerated framework. A matrix-free treecode (MFTC)-RBF strategy is designed to address mapping bottlenecks. It mitigates network latency and synchronization overhead caused by cross-node irregular communication via asynchronous computation-communication overlap. Furthermore, it resolves GPU instruction pipeline stalls induced by transcendental functions using a spatially-decoupled mixed-precision scheme combined with Horner polynomial approximation. To maximize intra-SM resource utilization and throughput, a dual-pipeline asynchronous scheduling (DAS) strategy is adopted to concurrently execute compute-bound and memory-bound tasks on Tensor and CUDA Cores. Evaluations show that MFTC-RBF delivers a 7.08x mapping speedup with scalability across 32,768 GPUs, while DAS hides approximately one-third of DGeMM latency. MFTC-RBF supports state-of-the-art mesh mapping with over 40-billion mesh points. End-to-end benchmarks further demonstrate a ~70% reduction in total runtime. Simulation results closely align with reference data in lead-cooled reactor benchmarks.

records.title: A Hardware Abstraction for Exascale Lattice Boltzmann Simulations: Rotor-Resolved Wind Farms on Aurora and LUMI
records.abstract: Developing performance-portable lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) codes for heterogeneous hardware without extensive hardware-specific duplication is challenging. We introduce a unified hardware abstraction within the open-source OpenLB framework. By expressing models against abstract cell-level concepts, this design enables compile-time binding to platform-specific data structures and common subexpression elimination across composed operators, yielding up to 2.5-fold speedups over an unoptimized baseline. We validate this approach using a rotor-resolved, wall-modeled large-eddy simulation (WMLES) of a 32-turbine wind farm, combining LBM with Brinkman penalization, moving walls and atmospheric boundary layer inflow. This complex fluid-structure interaction executes across NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs from a single-source implementation without hardware-specific modifications. At extreme scale, we execute the simulation on up to 2,048 Aurora nodes, achieving 86% weak scaling efficiency against a single node. Resolving 5.9 trillion cells at 51 trillion cell updates per second, this is the largest GPU-accelerated LBM simulation reported to date.

records.title: TokaGLINT: A Scalable GPU-Tailored Implicit Solver for Full 3D Tokamak Electromagnetic Simulations
records.abstract: We introduce TokaGLINT, a GPU-accelerated implicit solver for electromagnetic field computations in full 3D tokamak simulations, aimed at efficient large-scale parallel GPU computing. Its central innovation lies in the co-design of hierarchical domain decomposition and a fast exact local solver, where hierarchical partitioning is tailored to match fine-grained intra-card subdomains and exploit the tensor-based solver dedicated to curvilinear-coordinate symplectic CN-FDTD-discretized 3D Maxwell equations. Backed by automated operator fusion and batching customized for the intra-card multi-subdomain structure, the solver decouples unknowns through discrete transformations and leverages tensor-structured computations to achieve high hardware utilization, while preserving the long-time stability characteristic of symplectic discretizations. TokaGLINT scales the electromagnetic field solve beyond 10,000 GPUs, achieving 90.1% weak and 53.9% strong scaling efficiency, while delivering a 2.67x single-node speedup over an unpreconditioned BiCGStab baseline (HIP-enabled HYPRE). It is validated in EAST tokamak simulations within the SymPIC plasma simulation code, enabling high-fidelity long-duration modeling.

records.title: SigmaTrace: Library-Agnostic Observability for CPU/GPU-Initiated RDMA Communication
records.abstract: RDMA networking enables low-latency, high-bandwidth communication on large systems. Despite its adoption, however, observability is lacking. Existing tools target specific communication libraries or only report aggregated data, missing per-operation behavior. The gap is widest for GPU-initiated networking, whose in-kernel RDMA operations are invisible to the host. We present SigmaTrace, a library-agnostic RDMA profiling framework providing fine-grained, per-operation visibility for CPU and GPU-initiated networking. It traces operations at the libibverbs/mlx5dv layers, the common denominator beneath communication libraries on InfiniBand and RoCE, and employs a low-overhead memory interposition technique that, to our knowledge, gives the first observability into GPU-initiated RDMA without source patching or binary instrumentation. Host-side tracing adds 1.3% overhead on NCCL AllReduce at 128 GPUs and under 2% on RCCL at 1,024 GPUs. On a persistent-kernel BFS and Mixture-of-Experts inference, SigmaTrace exposes an in-kernel barrier spread and 2.13x inter-node traffic skew invisible to existing profilers.

records.title: LRCCL: Rethinking Collective Communication for Long-Haul RDMA Networks
records.abstract: Long-haul RDMA links operate at millisecond-scale round-trip times that break the assumptions baked into collective communication stacks designed for microsecond-scale-datacenter networks. We rethink the collective communication stack for this regime and present LRCCL, a long-haul-RDMA-based collective communication library co-designed across three layers. First, through the first systematic characterization of collective communication on the real-world ESnet long-haul RDMA, we identify three dimensions that govern collective performance: inter-node round count, per-round data scaling, and inter-rank timing skew induced by mixed intra/inter-node work. Second, we propose a split-plane transport design specifically for long-haul RDMA, with a software reliability combining automatic repeat request and forward error correction. Third, we identify long-haul-friendly collective algorithms guided by the three dimensions. On a real ESnet long-haul testbed, LRCCL achieves 4.2x-22.6x speedup over MPICH+UCX's default RC transport under the same collective algorithm and 2.0x-3.4x end-to-end speedup on NPB and LLM workloads, including under injected moderate and burst loss.

records.title: Provisioning Networks for AI Supercomputers: A Trace-Driven Study of Performance Sensitivity at Unprecedented Scale
records.abstract: AI workloads on supercomputers make interconnect performance a primary design constraint. Hardware specifications and microbenchmarks alone do not show how real workloads respond to latency, bandwidth, and jitter. We present a trace-driven study of network sensitivity for training and inference workloads at scales up to 4,096 GPUs. Our methodology combines signature-based trace decomposition with linear programming to make broad network-parameter sweeps feasible. It preserves the recorded NCCL schedules and program dependencies, and estimates a lower bound on runtime under the LogGP model. We validate the compositional analysis against monolithic linear programs, LogGOPSim, and hardware measurements at feasible scales. The resulting latency-bandwidth envelopes identify low-sensitivity regions and performance cliffs that vary substantially across workloads. They also show when bandwidth upgrades provide meaningful returns and when additional network performance has little effect. These results translate execution traces into practical guidance for evaluating network configurations while making the model assumptions explicit.

records.title: Faithful Prediction of the Performance of rocHPL Despite Hardware and Software Complexity
records.abstract: High Performance LINPACK (HPL) remains the primary benchmark for ranking supercomputers and often serves as a dimensioning design component for system constructors. Its performance depends on a wide variety of parameters and remains difficult to predict on large, modern, heterogeneous clusters. Using stochastic performance models of computational kernels and the network simulation capabilities of SimGrid, a simulation framework for parallel application performance prediction, we design a lightweight simulator of the implementation of HPL on AMD GPUs (rocHPL). Taking advantage of the structure of HPL, we reduce the simulation complexity by several orders of magnitude. We evaluate the predictive capability of our approach across four distinct accelerated platforms comprising up to 1,024 GPUs, two software releases, and a wide range of parameters, and demonstrate its accuracy (simulated and real executions differ by 4% on average), flexibility, and scalability (at this scale, simulations take less than an hour on a laptop).

records.title: Accelerating SpGEMM Through Lightweight Clustering and Cache-Aware Accumulation
records.abstract: Sparse matrix-matrix multiplication is one of the most crucial kernels in linear algebra solvers, graph analytics, and machine learning workloads. The clustered row-row style has emerged as a favorable SpGEMM workflow because of its potentially good parallelism. However, due to frequent data movement caused by irregular memory access, existing approaches often suffer from three issues: (1) workload imbalance and prohibitive preprocessing overhead, (2) unsatisfactory data locality, and (3) inefficient accumulation strategy. To this end, we propose LeSpGEMM, a locality-enhanced SpGEMM algorithm. LeSpGEMM introduces a lightweight row-clustering method to improve spatial locality with near-linear complexity, and a cache-aware hybrid accumulation strategy to exploit data reuse across diverse sparse patterns. It further incorporates optimized kernels, including a SIMD-accelerated dense accumulator and an efficient hash-based accumulator. Experimental results on multiple platforms show that LeSpGEMM significantly outperforms six state-of-the-art implementations while maintaining low preprocessing overhead.

records.title: Tackling Parallelization Challenges of Randomized Preconditioners with Dependency Tracking
records.abstract: Incomplete Cholesky (IC) is a common memory-efficient preconditioner for large graph Laplacian systems, but classical IC can break down on irregular graphs. Approximate Cholesky (AC) addresses this with randomized dropping that is provably breakdown-free. Its stochastic fill-in pattern, however, resists static parallelization, creating a "setup bottleneck." We present ParAC, which parallelizes the AC sampling rule of Gao, Kyng, and Spielman using dynamic dependency tracking and architecture-aware memory management to execute it efficiently on CPUs and GPUs while preserving its numerical updates. Total time-to-solution speedups over deterministic IC reach 57.3× on CPU and 52.2× on GPU. Algebraic multigrid (AMG) generally remains preferable on structured PDE discretizations. On the irregular graph Laplacians tested, ParAC is up to 7.2× faster than AMG on CPUs and 6.0× faster on GPUs. On 200 heterogeneous SDDM systems, ParAC converges on every instance, whereas the AMG solvers fail on 15 and 19, on CPU and GPU, respectively.

records.title: ReLATE: Accelerating Tensor Decomposition via Safe and Efficient Learning of Sparse Encodings
records.abstract: Tensor decomposition (TD) is essential for analyzing high-dimensional sparse data, yet its irregular computations and memory-access patterns pose major performance challenges on modern parallel processors. Prior works rely on expert-designed sparse tensor formats that fail to adapt to irregular tensor shapes and data distributions. We present the reinforcement-learned adaptive tensor encoding (ReLATE) framework, a learning-augmented method that discovers safe and efficient sparse encodings, without labeled examples, via a hybrid model-free and model-based algorithm that learns from both real and imagined actions. Moreover, ReLATE introduces elastic training, rule-driven action masking, and dynamics-informed action filtering to ensure correct encoding with bounded execution time, even during early learning. After offline training, with geometric-mean overhead of only 5.82% relative to TD workflow time, ReLATE deploys the best encoding with zero inference overhead. Across diverse real-world sparse tensors, ReLATE consistently outperforms the best expert-designed format by up to 2×, with a geometric-mean speedup of 1.38×–1.41×.

records.title: FastMPK: Unleashing Cache Reuse for Sparse Matrix Power Kernels on Many-Core Architectures
records.abstract: Many applications rely on the sparse matrix power kernel (MPK), which evaluates a short sequence of sparse matrix-vector multiplications (SpMVs) with the same matrix. MPK is therefore dominated by the memory traffic of repeatedly streaming the sparse matrix, and cache reuse across successive SpMVs offers a major opportunity to reduce data movement. However, exploiting such reuse introduces inter-SpMV dependencies that can severely restrict parallelism and induce frequent global synchronization, especially on GPUs. This paper presents FastMPK, a cache-aware MPK designed to run efficiently on both CPUs and GPUs. FastMPK models the matrix as a dependency graph, recursively partitions it into cache-resident subgraphs, and constructs a separator subgraph to decouple cross-subgraph dependencies and recover parallel work. A dependency-preserving runtime schedule maximizes immediate cache reuse while a multi-granularity parallelization strategy enables scalability on many-core processors. Evaluated on diverse architectures, FastMPK delivers average speedups of up to 1.84× over state-of-the-art implementations.

records.title: Improving Progressive Compression with Adaptive Interpolation and Coefficient Decomposition
records.abstract: Exascale simulations generate data far faster than it can be stored or analyzed, making efficient data reduction essential. Error-controlled lossy compression offers high compression ratios under user-specified error bounds, but the target tolerance must be fixed at compression time. Progressive compression relaxes this restriction, yet existing methods still rely on fixed refactoring strategies and do not fully exploit correlations among decomposed coefficients, limiting the efficiency of progressive retrieval. In this work, we present an adaptive progressive compression framework that improves retrieval efficiency for two common targets, namely error-bound and peak signal-to-noise ratios.

records.title: BlockMGARD: Accelerating Adaptive Scientific Data Reduction with Region-of-Interest Error Control on GPUs
records.abstract: The growing scale of scientific data makes lossy compression essential for reducing data volume under controllable error. Transformation-based compressors using multilevel decomposition, such as MGARD, achieve strong compression ratios but map poorly to GPU architectures. We propose BlockMGARD, an adaptive, region-of-interest (ROI)-supported GPU lossy compressor, with four contributions: (1) an In-cache Block decomposition leveraging GPU on-chip memory and constant lookup tables to accelerate decomposition; (2) a hybrid hierarchy combining In-cache Block and global decomposition to balance speed and compression ratio; (3) an end-to-end pipeline with fine-grained ROI error control for feature preservation; and (4) an evaluation against state-of-the-art methods on five real-world datasets. Compared to MGARD-X, BlockMGARD achieves up to 4.2x and 9.1x higher compression and decompression throughput, and up to 8.63x higher compression ratio than uniform-tolerance baselines under ROI-aware error control. Across four GPUs, BlockMGARD achieves near-ideal linear scaling and up to 1.58× I/O cost reduction over MGARD-X.

records.title: TOPIQ: Statistical Error Propagation for Quantity-of-Interest Prediction Under Lossy Compression
records.abstract: Lossy compression is essential for managing massive scientific data, but per-element error bounds do not translate into bounds on downstream quantities of interest (QoIs) such as regional averages, neural network predictions, or multi-field derived quantities. We present TOPIQ, a statistical error-propagation framework that predicts QoI-level bias and uncertainty from compact compression metadata (less than 0.1% of original data). TOPIQ decomposes QoIs into primitive operators with closed-form propagation rules accounting for spatial error correlation and data-error coupling; new QoIs are supported by composition at runtime with no per-QoI derivation or retraining. Across 552 evaluations spanning four datasets, three compressors, four QoI families, and eight error bounds, 93.1% of configurations achieve well-calibrated predictions. Pre-computed metadata enables post-hoc uncertainty quantification for arbitrary query regions at 56x-402x speedup over direct computation. A case study demonstrates integration into an AI-driven analysis pipeline with end-to-end confidence intervals for dynamically composed queries.

records.title: From Error-Bounded to Fixed-Ratio: Efficient Sampling-Guided GPU Lossy Compression
records.abstract: Modern high performance computing (HPC) applications generate massive datasets, creating memory pressure and costly data movement that hinder scientific discovery and AI innovation. GPU lossy compression reduces data volume, but existing approaches face limitations. Error-bounded compression provides strict quality guarantees but produces unpredictable compressed sizes, complicating memory provisioning and system integration. Fixed-ratio compression ensures predictable memory requirements but lacks explicit error control, potentially compromising data fidelity. We introduce MILIO, a GPU lossy compression framework that combines fixed-ratio control with error-bounded compression. Built on dimension-aware sampling, fine-grained ratio profiling, and multi-stream global synchronization, MILIO achieves user-specified compression ratios with high throughput while supporting error control. Across nine real-world scientific datasets, MILIO achieves a compression throughput of 257.1 GB/s on an NVIDIA A100 GPU, delivering 3.25× the throughput of cuZFP at comparable compression ratios. It integrates seamlessly with scientific and AI workloads and demonstrates near-optimal scalability across multiple GPUs.

records.title: FSZ: Breaking the Prediction-Throughput Trade-Off in GPU Lossy Compression
records.abstract: Existing fast GPU error-bounded lossy compressors achieve high throughput with pure-GPU single-kernel designs, but their compression ratios remain limited because they apply a fixed first-order predictor on independent blocks. We propose FSZ, a GPU error-bounded lossy compressor that redesigns the prediction stage with three innovations within a single CUDA kernel: (1) cross-block prediction state carries Lorenzo state across block boundaries within 256-element tiles, eliminating seven of eight boundary residuals; (2) per-tile adaptive multi-order prediction and centering selects the best strategy for each tile; and (3) a single-pass four-way evaluation exploits a property of finite differences to evaluate all variants from one data read, within a fixed predictor's bandwidth budget. On NVIDIA GH200 with eight real-world datasets, FSZ outperforms cuSZp-P by up to 10.95x and cuSZp-O by up to 2.92x in compression ratio while achieving the highest average throughput (676 GB/s compression, 785 GB/s decompression) among all evaluated compressors.

records.title: Do We Need Tensor Cores for Stencil Computations?
records.abstract: Stencil computation is a fundamental kernel in scientific computing, widely used in applications such as fluid dynamics and weather simulation. Although stencils are traditionally considered memory-bound and thus ill-suited for compute-oriented Tensor Cores, recent studies report substantial acceleration, creating an apparent contradiction. This paper resolves this discrepancy through a systematic performance analysis of stencil computations on Tensor Cores. We revisit stencil-to-Tensor-Core mappings, quantify the computational redundancy introduced by hardware-driven transformations, and develop an enhanced performance model that captures arithmetic-intensity shifts under temporal fusion. From this model, we derive analytical criteria that provide a first-order estimate of whether Tensor Cores will outperform, match, or underperform CUDA Cores for a given stencil and hardware setting. Our analysis identifies the performance sweet spot for Tensor Core acceleration. Evaluations on NVIDIA GPUs with state-of-the-art implementations, including EBISU, ConvStencil, and SPIDER, validate our criteria and show its value for guiding stencil optimization.

records.title: Unleashing Shared Memory Potential for NEP Machine-Learning Potential in Molecular Dynamics on GPUs
records.abstract: Machine-learning potentials (MLPs) achieve near first-principles accuracy in molecular dynamics while retaining high efficiency. The neuroevolution potential (NEP) uses compact networks to deliver substantially higher GPU throughput than other MLPs. However, existing NEP implementations suffer from high per-thread memory demands that limit effective use of low-latency shared memory. We present a shared-memory-centric optimization framework for NEP on GPUs. By introducing subwarp partitioning and two-dimensional neighbor reordering, it enhances inter-thread data sharing and reduces memory requirements, allowing most accesses to be served from shared memory. We further incorporate shared-memory-based matricized computation, buffering strategies, along with a series of GPU performance optimizations, and quantify shared memory usage to facilitate analysis. Our framework achieves up to 18.09x speedup over the baseline GPU implementation and an average of 2.60x speedup over GPUMD across five representative material systems on NVIDIA H100 GPUs.

records.title: Every Microsecond Matters: Achieving Near-Speed-of-Light Latency in GPU Collectives
records.abstract: GPU collective communication is often optimized for bandwidth, yet many emerging workloads are latency-bound. Long-context LLM inference is a key example, where small collectives lie on the critical path of token generation, making microsecond-scale overheads impactful. In this work, we study how to approach the hardware speed-of-light (SoL) lower bound for GPU collectives within a scale-up network. We identify key design principles, including barrier-free synchronization and efficient use of symmetric memory and multicast. Building on NCCL’s device-side API, we develop low-latency interfaces for constructing custom kernels and implement new symmetric collectives in NCCL. Microbenchmarks show substantial latency reductions, achieving within 10% of the measured SoL bound. Integrated into applications, these kernels reduce inter-token latency and improve throughput in LLM inference, while also accelerating cuSOLVERMp, demonstrating benefits across AI and HPC workloads.

records.title: CoreFlow: Context-Centric Resource Management for LLM-Based Agentic Workflows
records.abstract: The rise of agentic workflows, which coordinate multiple LLM-based agents to tackle complex tasks, has shifted the LLM serving toward a multi-step, context-driven execution paradigm. This shift introduces highly skewed context-length distributions and agent-specific KV cache-reuse patterns in LLM workloads, challenging existing resource management systems that remain oblivious to these characteristics. This paper introduces CoreFlow, a context-centric resource management system tailored for the distinct execution patterns of agentic workflows. CoreFlow incorporates three key designs: (1) hierarchical performance modeling, which captures the effects of context-length variance and imbalanced cache reuse inherent in context-driven execution; (2) dual-level resource optimization, combining workflow-level allocation to distribute resources across agents with agent-level partitioning to isolate requests with heterogeneous context lengths; and (3) adaptive cache management, which aligns cache placement with resource partitioning while minimizing cache-swap overhead. Evaluations on representative workflows demonstrate that CoreFlow reduces end-to-end latency by 57.6% and improves workflow throughput by 63.1%.

records.title: Expert-as-a-Service: Towards Efficient, Scalable, and Robust Large-Scale MoE Serving
records.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models challenge serving infrastructures with dynamic, sparse expert utilization, causing instability on conventional systems designed for dense architectures. We propose EaaS, a novel serving system to enable efficient, scalable, and robust MoE deployment. Our system disaggregates MoE modules into independent, stateless services. This design enables fine-grained resource scaling and provides inherent fault tolerance by decoupling compute units. The architecture is powered by a high-performance, CPU-free peer-to-peer communication library that ensures minimal overhead and high throughput. Experiments confirm EaaS's scalability and efficiency, achieving performance comparable to monolithic systems while providing robust fault tolerance and strong scalability. EaaS incurs less than a 2% throughput reduction under simulated hardware failures that would otherwise halt monolithic architectures. It further saves up to 37.5% of computing resources through dynamic fine-grained adaptation to serving traffic, demonstrating strong resilience for large-scale MoE deployment in production.

records.title: Prefill-Decode Aggregation or Disaggregation? Unifying Both for Goodput-Optimized LLM Serving
records.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving has long centered on a debate between prefill-decode (PD) aggregation and disaggregation. We systematically compare them under joint time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT) service-level objectives (SLOs): aggregation wins when TTFT SLOs are tight and TPOT SLOs relaxed; disaggregation wins in the opposite regime. Under balanced SLOs, however, both are significantly suboptimal in SLO-compliant throughput (goodput), revealing a previously uncharacterized gap. We attribute this gap to unexploited latency slack: many requests complete well within SLOs while others approach violation. We propose latency shifting, a design principle for reallocating SLO slack across requests and phases to maximize goodput. TaiChi, an LLM serving system, unifies aggregation and disaggregation through hybrid-mode inference to realize this principle through flowing decode and length-aware prefill scheduling. TaiChi improves goodput by up to 40% and reduces P90 TTFT and TPOT by up to 5.3× and 1.6×, respectively, over state-of-the-art aggregation and disaggregation systems.

records.title: When KV Meets Embeddings: Dynamic GPU Memory Allocation for Accelerating Generative Recommender Serving
records.abstract: Generative recommender (GR) inference faces a dual memory bottleneck absent in LLM serving. Embedding hot caches and KV caches compete for limited GPU HBM, while existing systems optimize them in isolation, leading to suboptimal tail latency. We observe that (1) the optimal EMB–KV memory allocation ratio shifts by up to 0.35 across workloads, and (2) static allocations leave 20%–30% latency improvement untapped, while continuous reallocation risks cache thrashing and P99 SLO violations. We present RACER, which jointly and adaptively allocates HBM at runtime. It addresses two challenges: (1) adaptive memory allocation via a three-layer PPO controller with online adaptation and burst recovery, achieving 32 μs decision latency; and (2) embedding-KV-aware scheduling that maximizes joint EMB–KV cache reuse across nodes. Evaluations on three production-scale datasets show that RACER reduces P99 latency by 24%–38% over the best static strategy and achieves 93.5%–99.6% SLO satisfaction, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines (67%–94.2%) without sacrificing throughput.

records.title: Efficient Serving for Agentic LLM Workflows via Micro-Task-Level Parallelism
records.abstract: Agentic large language model (LLM) workflows leverage the advanced capabilities of LLMs to instantiate a multi-agent paradigm, where each LLM invocation constitutes an agentic task. Existing optimizations rely on coarse-grained task-level scheduling, which fails to exploit fine-grained parallelism within the workflow, leading to resource underutilization and bursty latency. In this paper, we present Grape, a full-stack LLM system for serving agentic LLM workflows that fully exploits micro-task (μTask)-level parallelism. On the frontend, Grape proposes the TaskFlow abstraction to provide a declarative interface for workflow orchestration. Subsequently, Grape decomposes tasks represented in TaskFlow into fine-grained μTasks that expose the parallelism within the workflow. For the LLM engine, Grape adopts a μTasks-aware scheduling policy with SLO-derived constraints to ensure low-latency execution with improved resource utilization. Moreover, Grape also proposes a dedicated memory management mechanism to alleviate KV Cache memory pressure. The experimental results demonstrate the superiority of Grape over state-of-the-art solutions.

records.title: MIST: A Co-Design Framework for Heterogeneous, Multi-Stage LLM Inference
records.abstract: Modern LLM serving spans multi-stage pipelines, including RAG retrieval and KV cache reuse, with distinct compute, memory, and latency demands. Inference engines expose vast configuration spaces with no systematic navigation methodology, and exhaustive benchmarking can exceed $40K in cloud costs. Meanwhile, hardware is diversifying across AMD GPUs, TPUs, and custom ASICs, yet cross-vendor prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation lacks a unified software stack for end-to-end evaluation. We present MIST, an event-driven simulation framework that models the full serving stack across AI workload, system and software, and hardware layers, with pluggable accelerator models enabling cross-vendor evaluation. MIST achieves end-to-end fidelity within 6% of real deployed systems. In design-space exploration case studies, under stated pricing and hardware assumptions, multi-vendor PD-disaggregated deployments identified by MIST yield up to 49.3% higher tokens/$ than single-vendor PD disaggregation. MIST also enables KV storage co-design, revealing how memory hierarchy choices shape tail latency. MIST is available at https://github.com/MIST-Simulator/MIST.

records.title: BidKV: Utility-Guided Preemption Scheduling for KV-Pressure LLM Serving
records.abstract: When key-value (KV) cache demand exceeds GPU memory in online large language model (LLM) serving, engines reclaim active requests' cache. Poor victim selection increases recomputation and time to first token (TTFT). We present BidKV, a utility-guided policy that ranks victims by recoverable capacity and estimated disruption cost. BidKV integrates with vLLM and SGLang through a portable adapter that reuses native preemption. With Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and ShareGPT traces, BidKV reduces 95th-percentile TTFT by over 90% and improves 300 ms service-level objective (SLO) attainment by 14.8 percentage points over vLLM's native policy. On SGLang, it reduces 95th-percentile TTFT by 94.6% and improves SLO attainment by 38.8 percentage points over native least-recently-used eviction. Source code is available at https://github.com/CGCL-codes/BidKV.

records.title: A Parallel Algorithm for the Construction of Partial Information Decomposition-Based Genome-Scale Networks from Single-Cell Datasets
records.abstract: Methods for constructing gene networks from tissue-level expression data, developed over the past two decades, are being reassessed for applicability to single-cell datasets. The higher noise and sparsity of single-cell data demand more robust, computationally intensive approaches, while also requiring scalability to orders-of-magnitude larger datasets. We focus on PIDC, an information-theoretic method that produces high-quality networks from single-cell data but incurs $O(n^3)$ runtime for $n$ genes, limiting scalability even with parallelization. We present a novel sequential algorithm that reduces complexity to $O(n^2 \log n)$, along with its distributed-memory parallelization achieving $O(n^2/p + T_{sort}(n^2, p))$ time, where $p$ is the number of processors and $T_{sort}$ is the time for parallel sorting. On 64 cores, our MPI implementation achieves a 158X speedup over the existing PIDC algorithm. We further demonstrate construction of a genome-scale human gene network with 30,000 genes from 800,000 cells in 2.5 hours using 2,048 cores.

records.title: Robust Score-Bounded Search for Multi-Hit Carcinogenic Gene Combination Identification
records.abstract: Cancer arises from combinations of somatic mutations (hits), and identifying these combinations is critical for understanding carcinogenesis and enabling targeted therapies. This task can be formulated as a weighted set cover problem, yet exhaustive enumeration leads to exponential search space growth as the number of hits increases, limiting prior enumeration-based work to at most five-hit combinations even on large-scale supercomputers. We propose a novel algorithm that decomposes higher-order combinations through a shortest addition chain and formulates sample coverage computation as matrix multiplication. It employs a robust score-bounded search strategy that eliminates unpromising candidates without evaluation, while guaranteeing that the best-scoring combination is never discarded. Experiments show our method visits less than one-millionth of prior search spaces, identifies four-hit combinations in about five seconds on a single GPU, outperforms thousand-node supercomputers by orders of magnitude, and extends practical reach of enumeration-based cancer screening from five-hit to nine-hit combinations.

records.title: RT-HiSS: Ray Tracing Accelerated High-Dimensional Vector Similarity Searches
records.abstract: Recent GPU generations include special-purpose ray tracing (RT) cores for graphics applications. While RT cores are primarily used for rendering, recent works show they can be leveraged for general-purpose tasks, including similarity searches. However, existing approaches do not support datasets exceeding three dimensions. In this work, we propose RT-HiSS, the first exact GPU RT-core-based similarity search algorithm for high-dimensional datasets. GPU similarity search often scales poorly for large datasets with substantial search distances. To address this, RT-HiSS uses RT cores for fast index construction and searches, followed by candidate refinement on CUDA cores. We introduce a two-pass approach to estimate an upper bound on result size, enabling efficient batching under GPU memory constraints with near-perfect load balancing. Additionally, we examine shared memory tiling and compressed result masks to improve GPU resource utilization. RT-HiSS yields speedups up to 8.37x over competitive state-of-the-art GPU algorithms across six real-world datasets.

records.title: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Scientific Particle Data Compression and Rendering
records.abstract: Large-scale particle simulations produce hundreds of millions of particles, straining storage, transfer, and interactive visualization. Existing lossy compressors such as SZ3 operate in data space and provide no guarantees on downstream visualization fidelity. We propose ParticleGS, a visualization-aware framework based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that learns a compact representation directly optimized for rendered image quality, combining (1) a multi-stage, multi-orbit training pipeline, (2) VizMapper, a lightweight network that adapts a single trained model to user-specified visualization parameters at inference time, and (3) spatial block training with KD-tree decomposition and global fine-tuning. On a 281-million-particle HACC cosmological simulation, our eight-block model reaches 30.03 dB PSNR at 65× compression, outperforming SZ3 by 5–8 dB at comparable ratios, and generalizes without tuning to additional HACC regions and a dark-matter-only FIRE-2 simulation. It renders at 662 FPS on a single GPU, over 2,300× faster than ParaView on the full particle data.

records.title: Mercury: Practical User-Space API Remoting for Secure Containers in Public Clouds
records.abstract: In public cloud environments, secure containers face challenges in device virtualization due to their micro virtual machine architecture. We introduce Mercury, a user-space API remoting framework co-designed with our secure container RunD. Mercury leverages a dynamic shared memory interface between guest and host, along with KVM hypercalls for efficient notifications. When applied to CUDA, Mercury preserves API semantics across virtualization boundaries, enabling GPU virtualization with under 4% overhead during large language model inference. Mercury also achieves a 20% speedup compared to existing API remoting solutions. Building on Mercury, we deploy GPU sharing and checkpoint/restore in Alibaba Cloud, effectively doubling GPU deployment density and reducing cold start latency by over 95% in practice.

records.title: No Disk Left Behind: Lifetime-Aware Oversubscription of Thin Provisioned Storage in Cloud IaaS Platforms
records.abstract: Cloud resource oversubscription is widely used to improve infrastructure utilization, particularly for CPU resources. In contrast, storage resources remain largely statically provisioned despite significant underutilization. Our analysis of multiple OVHcloud platforms shows that virtual machines use on average only 42.9% of their local disk capacity. In this paper, we explore disk oversubscription in thin-provisioned environments. Unlike CPU, storage resources are persistent and difficult to predict in the black-box context of IaaS platforms. To address these challenges, we introduce Wave, a dynamic oversubscription method that anticipates waves of disk capacity released by virtual machine (VM) churn. Using large-scale traces from OVHcloud, we show that Wave can reduce required disk capacity by up to 2× while maintaining a low rate of corrective migrations. Beyond infrastructure efficiency, this reduction translates into significant environmental benefits, lowering storage-related Scope 3 emissions by approximately 44.5% in newer cloud regions.

records.title: HolyDiver: Water and Carbon Footprint-Aware Serverless Computing
records.abstract: This paper introduces HolyDiver, a serverless function scheduling and execution strategy that jointly optimizes the carbon footprint, water footprint, and service time of serverless functions. HolyDiver is the first system to navigate the challenging three-way trade-off among these competing objectives by leveraging spatio-temporal variations in the environmental factors that impact the carbon and water footprint of electricity generation, datacenter operation, and cooling. To solve this optimization problem, HolyDiver demonstrates a novel application of Harris Hawks Optimization (HHO) and extends HHO with dynamic hawk count adjustment, water scarcity-aware scheduling, and peer-guided performance estimation to adapt to the rapidly changing environmental conditions and function invocation patterns inherent to serverless environments. HolyDiver is evaluated on a cluster of nodes distributed across 10 regions with production-grade function execution traces and established benchmarks. We observe that HolyDiver consistently approaches the optimal solution and can complement existing schedulers to reduce the environmental footprint of serverless computing.

records.title: Policy-Constrained Delegated Access for HPC
records.abstract: High performance computing systems rely on a direct user-access model: users authenticate at the access boundary and operate within Unix accounts. This model supports strong attribution and bounded privilege but does not address the growing role of software that accesses clusters on behalf of users. Science gateways, workflow systems, and remote development tools initiate SSH-mediated actions without per-connection user involvement. Existing delegation mechanisms such as shared credentials and long-lived keys weaken auditability and complicate enforcement. This paper treats delegated cluster access as an access-control problem at the HPC access boundary. We present a policy-constrained signer that validates the user's identity, maps requests to site-defined Unix principals, and issues short-lived SSH certificates scoped by policy. Standard OpenSSH login nodes enforce these certificates with no additional software. We evaluate the signer on a Jetstream2 SLURM testbed across issuance overhead, enforcement, revocation, and auditability. We separately evaluate certificate-based workflow resilience under connection drops.

records.title: DySpin: A Plug-and-Play Library Advancing Dynamic Sparse Long-Context Inference
records.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is constrained by the memory-bandwidth and capacity demands of the key-value (KV) cache. Existing sparse methods typically use fixed per-head token budgets, overlooking variations in runtime demand. Moreover, since they retain all tokens in memory, these methods do not alleviate GPU memory capacity constraints. To overcome these limitations, we present DySpin, a plug-and-play library for dynamic sparse long-context inference. Its training-free runtime allocator dynamically adjusts token budgets to preserve important tokens and improve accuracy. To address the resulting workload imbalance, FastEstimate fuses token-importance evaluation and selection to generate scheduling indices that guide a specialized decoding attention kernel for fine-grained load balancing. DySpin further employs six-bit KV cache quantization and a novel packing format that enables register-level parallel unpacking and dequantization, reducing both dequantization overhead and memory footprint. DySpin integrates with existing sparse frameworks, improving accuracy while reducing long-context inference latency and KV cache memory usage.

records.title: SwarmLoRA: Serverless Shared-Computation Disaggregation for Isolated, High-Throughput Multi-LoRA Serving
records.abstract: Over 100,000 public LoRA adapters now share a small number of base LLMs, and cloud providers increasingly serve them for independent tenants whose private data must stay isolated. Serverful systems co-locate all adapters in one process for efficient batching but sacrifice isolation; serverless systems run each adapter in an isolated function but redundantly recompute the shared base-model projection in every one, wasting GPU memory bandwidth. We present SwarmLoRA, a disaggregated serverless architecture that separates shared computation from per-adapter state. A persistent aggregator batches the base-model projection once across all active functions; isolated worker functions each hold one adapter’s weights and KV cache and scale independently. This design achieves cross-adapter batching without breaking per-adapter isolation. SwarmLoRA achieves 4.1×-4.9× higher throughput on four L40S GPUs than state-of-the-art ServerlessLLM and ServerlessLoRA, while preventing cross-tenant data leakage through malicious adapters. SwarmLoRA shows that multi-tenant LoRA serving need not trade tenant isolation for batching efficiency.

records.title: DOLPHIN: Scalable Disk-RAM-GPU Pipelined Training for Massive Temporal GNNs
records.abstract: Temporal graph neural networks (T-GNNs) play a key role in modeling dynamic graphs by learning representations that capture evolving structures and interactions. However, scaling T-GNNs remains challenging, as massive real-world graphs and complex temporal dependencies incur prohibitive runtime and memory costs. Existing systems often preload entire datasets into RAM and rely on RAM-GPU pipelines, suffering from batch-boundary pipeline bubbles, thereby limiting throughput. In this paper, we present DOLPHIN, a scalable Disk-RAM-GPU pipelined system for massive T-GNNs. DOLPHIN groups training batches into chunks and incorporates two key techniques: an I/O-efficient feature window scheduler for just-in-time Disk-to-RAM chunk provisioning, and a dependency-graph–based parallel execution plan that improves GPU utilization while preserving model quality. Together, these techniques improve pipeline efficiency across the Disk-RAM-GPU memory hierarchy and computation phases. Experiments on six real-world graphs show DOLPHIN delivers up to 21.07x faster training and reduces RAM usage by up to 92.04% compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

records.title: hZCCL2: Co-Designing Collective Communication with Vectorized Homomorphic Compression
records.abstract: Inter-node collective communication is a dominant bottleneck in large-scale scientific simulations and distributed artificial-intelligence workloads. Prior frameworks mitigate this via error-bounded lossy compression but face fundamental limits: scalar encoding underutilizes memory bandwidth, and outliers inflate fixed-length blocks, leaving compression ratio (CR) untapped at SIMD-friendly block sizes. We present hZCCL2, a co-designed framework that optimizes SIMD encoding, homomorphic compression, and collective communication. Its HVZ compressor achieves up to 5.31x higher compression throughput than prior state-of-the-art compressors and improves CR by up to 37.6% at SIMD-friendly block sizes with outlier-aware encoding. Its homomorphic compression is up to 8.1x faster than the decompress-operate-compress workflow. Evaluated on 3,584 CPU cores, hZCCL2 reaches up to 47.2x Bcast, 23.4x Scatter, 43.8x Allreduce, and 67.6x Alltoall peak speedups over native MPI. In an image-stacking application, it achieves 12.9x speedup at a single thread and 39.5x at 112 threads while preserving the user-specified error bound.

records.title: Scaling Spatiotemporal Generative Compression for Earth Observation on an HPC-AI-Converged Supercomputer
records.abstract: Earth observation constellations generate multispectral data at unprecedented rates, creating storage and distribution bottlenecks. To reduce storage and accelerate global dissemination, we propose a scalable two-stage generative compression framework validated on annual global Sentinel-2 imagery. The encoding stage exploits large-scale spatial context and temporal redundancy, while the reconstruction stage restores the multispectral latent space and uses geolocation and observation time as metadata controls to guide generation with global historical priors. To meet the computational and memory demands of training global-scale generative models, we redesign the framework for an HPC-AI-converged supercomputer. Through topology-aware hierarchical parallelization, asymmetric HBM-DDR memory placement, and asynchronous overlap execution on Armv9 and SME, our implementation achieves end-to-end training performance comparable to high-end A100 GPU platforms under the reported workload and scales to 20,480 LineShine nodes with 76% weak-scaling efficiency. It achieves over 4,700x archive compression, outperforming existing compression methods in downstream land-cover classification.

records.title: CoCoDiff: Optimizing Collective Communications for Distributed Diffusion Transformer Inference Under Ulysses Sequence Parallelism
records.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) are increasingly adopted in scientific computing, yet growing model sizes and resolutions make distributed multi-GPU inference essential. Ulysses sequence parallelism scales DiT inference but introduces frequent all-to-all collectives that dominate latency. Overlapping these with computation is difficult due to tight data dependencies, large messages, and asymmetric interconnect bandwidths. We introduce CoCoDiff, a distributed DiT inference engine exploiting two observations: (1) V requires only linear projection while Q/K need additional normalization and RoPE, enabling overlap of V's communication with Q/K computation; (2) adjacent denoising steps produce similar tensors, yielding temporal redundancy. CoCoDiff introduces three mechanisms: Tile-Aware Parallel All-to-all (TAPA) decomposes collectives into topology-aligned phases; V-First scheduling hides V's communication behind Q/K computation; and V-Major selective communication transmits only active projections on slow interconnects. On Aurora with four DiT models across 1–8 nodes (up to 96 Intel GPU tiles), CoCoDiff achieves an average speedup of 3.6×, peaking at 8.4×.

records.title: SpCCL: A Sparsity-Aware Collective Communication Library for GPU Platforms
records.abstract: Collective communication is essential to high performance computing and machine learning workloads, yet libraries such as NCCL do not exploit sparsity in message payloads. Sending only nonzero values can reduce network traffic, but explicitly handling sparsity introduces challenges such as compression and decompression overheads. We address these challenges with sparsity-exploiting versions of all-gather, reduce-scatter, and all-reduce collectives. Our implementations use a new bitvector-based format, Pici, designed for low space overhead and fast GPU-based compression and decompression. Further, our collective algorithms adapt to the degree of sparsity in data, modifying data representations during the course of the collective. At 99% input sparsity, our collectives achieve up to 5.25×, 2.5×, and 2.66× speedups over NCCL for all-gather, reduce-scatter, and all-reduce, respectively. Integrating our collectives into a representative deep learning application, we achieve a 26% end-to-end speedup.

records.title: FluidGPU: Fine-Grained Kernel Disaggregation for Large Model Inference on Heterogeneous GPUs
records.abstract: This paper presents FluidGPU, the first kernel disaggregation system to improve performance and cost efficiency on heterogeneous GPUs for large model inference. Our key insight is that kernels within a single application exhibit diverse resource demands, making them the most suitable granularity for aligning computation with hardware capabilities. FluidGPU integrates offline analysis with online adaptation by extracting precise inter-kernel dependencies from PTX to ensure correctness, overlapping communication with computation through a pipelined execution model, and employing workload-aware scheduling with lightweight runtime adaptation. Extensive evaluations across five heterogeneous GPUs and four model architectures, scaling up to 16 GPUs, show that FluidGPU improves serving throughput and cost efficiency by up to 2.3× and 1.6×, respectively, compared to existing disaggregation methods, while generalizing to model architectures where prior approaches do not apply. Surprisingly, a heterogeneous GPU pair under FluidGPU can even exceed the throughput of two homogeneous high-end GPUs at a lower cost.

records.title: How Much Can Large Language Models Optimize Job Management in HPC Systems？
records.abstract: Large language models are increasingly capable, yet their integration into HPC job management remains limited. This paper identifies three optimization opportunities across the job lifecycle: resource demand prediction at submission, adaptive backfill parameter reconfiguration during scheduling, and anomaly diagnosis during execution. We build a unified framework combining domain-specific supervised fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation, and agentic workflows, and further incorporate rigorous hallucination mitigation mechanisms to ensure safe and reliable deployment. Extensive experiments on multiple open-source and proprietary LLMs using several historical datasets demonstrate that our domain-specific models can consistently improve job resource demand prediction accuracy, enhance scheduling efficiency via online reconfiguration of backfill parameters, and provide interpretable root-cause triage through a dual-agent workflow. Ultimately, this work establishes a foundational step toward intelligent HPC environments.

records.title: ZOCheck: CPU-Shadow Checkpointing for Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning
records.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization is an attractive option for memory-efficient LLM fine-tuning, but its fault tolerance remains underexplored. Unlike first-order training, ZO progress can be represented by lightweight seed-and-scalar step logs, yet naive log-only recovery still incurs replay cost that grows with training progress, and shortcut replay does not preserve the executed floating-point trajectory. We present ZOCheck, a fault-tolerant ZO training system that exploits this replayable structure through a CPU shadow process that continuously replays logged updates, materializes consistent recovery images off the GPU critical path, and persists them asynchronously. ZOCheck combines non-blocking checkpointing with fast recovery from a near-current state. We also develop a cost model for choosing the snapshot policy under realistic failure rates. Experiments show that ZOCheck reduces checkpoint overhead by up to 219.7× and recovery latency by 1.55× on average over asynchronous full-state checkpointing, yielding up to 21.3× lower end-to-end wasted time while preserving exact recovery behavior.

records.title: Maze: A Distributed Framework for Large Language Model Agents
records.abstract: LLM agents are transitioning from single-node to large-scale, multi-tenant services. A user request no longer corresponds to a single inference call, but to a long-running workflow interleaving heterogeneous tasks. Existing agent systems struggle with these workloads due to resource-blind, coarse-grained placement or ignore agentic workload awareness. We present Maze, a distributed agent framework bridging the abstraction gap from agentic logic to fine-grained task-level deployment. At its core, Maze anchors task resource semantics and introduces Heterogeneity-Aware Criticality Scheduler, a scheduler leveraging agentic workload features and value-density scoring to prioritize valuable agentic workflows and critical tasks while eliminating cross-resource head-of-line blocking. Coupled with elastic inference engine scaling, zero-VRAM optimizations, and closed-loop fault tolerance, Maze ensures a robust, performant runtime. Evaluation on diverse workloads demonstrates that Maze achieves up to 2.9x higher throughput, reduces P95 latency by 54.2%, and increases GPU utilization by 50% compared to state-of-the-art frameworks.

records.title: Evaluation and Optimization of Communication Compression for 10K-GPU LLM Training
records.abstract: Collective communication is critical for scaling large language model (LLM) training to megascale GPU clusters. However, communication becomes a major bottleneck limiting scalability. Existing approaches improve bandwidth utilization but are constrained by the physical network in large-scale clusters. Communication compression reduces data volume and offers a way to break the communication wall, yet its performance and accuracy at extreme scale remain unclear. To bridge this gap, we present the first systematic study of communication compression across scales up to 10K GPUs, showing that it maintains accuracy but suffers from limited performance gains due to bandwidth hierarchy limitations, weak communication scaling, and limited resource awareness. We enhance the co-design of communication and compression with a hierarchical method that restructures communication compression, adapts communication algorithms to each scale, and tunes network resource allocation. Our approach achieves up to 5.87x communication improvement and 1.73x end-to-end training speedup on Llama3 models at 10,240 GPUs.

records.title: RailX: A Flexible, Scalable, and Low-Cost Network Architecture for Hyper-Scale AI Workloads
records.abstract: The exponential growth of AI models necessitates hyper-scale networking infrastructures with unprecedented cost-effectiveness and scalability. However, traditional packet-switched fat-trees are prohibitively expensive, while direct circuit-switched topologies exhibit poor scalability and limited all-to-all performance. In this paper, we present a novel reconfigurable network architecture called RailX that achieves high scalability, high performance, high flexibility, and low cost simultaneously. RailX organizes nodes and optical switches in a 2D configuration, achieving much better scalability than existing centralized circuit switching networks. We propose a novel interconnection method based on Hamiltonian decomposition theory to organize separate rail-based rings into all-to-all topologies, simultaneously optimizing both ring-collective and all-to-all communication at ultra-scale. RailX's flat switching layer interconnects over 400K high-bandwidth chips with a diameter of just 2-4 inter-node hops. It slashes costs per all-reduce and all-to-all bandwidth to under 10% and 50% of fat-trees, respectively. For MLaaS, we flexibly map diverse AI workloads and bypass hardware failures.

records.title: NCCLZ: Compression-Enabled GPU Collectives with Decoupled Quantization and Entropy Coding
records.abstract: Collective communication is a major bottleneck for multi-node GPU workloads in scientific computing and distributed deep learning, especially when inter-node bandwidth is limited. Although NCCL provides optimized GPU-centric collectives, large messages can still dominate end-to-end performance. Existing compression-enabled collective libraries either rely on MPI-based stacks that cannot fully exploit NCCL, omit entropy coding, or tightly couple full compressors with communication primitives, limiting compression ratio, flexibility, and communication-computation overlap. This paper presents NCCLZ, a compression-enabled GPU collective that decouples quantization and entropy coding and integrates them at different layers of the stack. NCCLZ places quantization at the interface, embeds entropy coding into NCCL primitives, uses a lightweight device-side selector to choose coding strategies, and overlaps compression with communication to reduce exposed overhead. Experiments on scientific datasets, training gradients, and synthetic workloads show up to 9.65x speedup over NCCL and up to 3.34x improvement over prior compression-assisted collective libraries.

records.title: Double-Precision Matrix Multiplication Emulation via Ozaki-II Scheme with FP8 Quantization
records.abstract: In this paper, we propose a method for emulating double-precision general matrix–matrix multiplication (DGEMM), a fundamental and performance-critical kernel in many high-performance computing applications. Ozaki-I and Ozaki-II are established DGEMM emulation schemes via low-precision matrix multiply-accumulate (MMA) units. For the Ozaki-I scheme, INT8-, FP8-, and FP16-based implementations have been proposed, all of which can be realized based on the same underlying algorithmic structure. In contrast, although INT8-based implementations of the Ozaki-II scheme have been reported, the original algorithm cannot be directly adapted to exploit FP8 MMA units. In several recent architectures, such as NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra and NVIDIA Rubin, INT8 performance has been reduced, making reliance on INT8 alone insufficient. Therefore, we introduce a novel technique to demonstrate DGEMM emulation based on the Ozaki-II scheme that operates on FP8 MMA units. Compared to the FP8-based Ozaki-I scheme, our method significantly reduces the computational cost and enables efficient FP64 emulation.

records.title: EmuGEMM: Fused Tensor Core Kernels for Precision Emulation in Matrix Multiplication
records.abstract: Modern GPUs devote an increasing silicon budget to low-precision matrix-multiplication units, widening the precision–throughput gap for scientific computing workloads. Ozaki Schemes I and II offer an alternative by reconstructing high-precision general matrix multiplication (GEMM) from low-precision operations, yet existing implementations leave substantial performance untapped. In particular, intermediate results are repeatedly materialized in global memory, making data movement the dominant bottleneck. We present EmuGEMM, fused integer Tensor Core kernels for NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs that eliminate redundant memory round-trips in both Ozaki schemes. Using Scheme I, EmuGEMM sustains up to 1,639 Top/s on Hopper (83% of INT8 peak) and 3,654 Top/s on Blackwell (81%). For large matrices, EmuGEMM surpasses cuBLAS TF32 throughput by up to 1.4× on Hopper and 1.7× on Blackwell, at comparable accuracy. Using Scheme II, EmuGEMM extends to complex arithmetic and outperforms cuBLAS ZGEMM by up to 2.3× on Hopper and 5.5× on Blackwell.

records.title: Pushing the Limits of Structured Sparse GEMM on Hopper GPUs via Analytical Modeling
records.abstract: Structured sparsity improves performance in LLM inference and scientific computing, yet Hopper 2:4 sparse GEMM remains poorly understood. Published kernel-level optimizations target older architectures, while no prior work investigates how Hopper's Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA), warpgroup execution, expanded shared memory, and asynchronous pipelines reshape the design space. We present an analytical model that captures roofline bounds, L2 reuse, pipeline overlap, and wave quantization for Hopper sparse GEMM. It serves as a guardrail for configuration search. Guided by the model, we develop an auto-tuned kernel combining warp-specialized TMA pipelining, metadata prepacking, barrier-decomposed overlap, and per-operand swizzles. On an H800 PCIe GPU, it outperforms cuSPARSELt on 80 of 95 shapes (84%) under identical problem configurations, with mean speedup of +16.7% and up to 1.4x. The model identifies memory bottlenecks and narrows the configuration space before compilation, reducing tuning cost while retaining high-performance configurations. This paper bridges both gaps.

records.title: Towards Exascale Fully Relativistic Pseudopotential Density Functional Theory Calculations with Mixed-Precision Computation and Compressed Communication Using Residual-Based Subspace Iteration
records.abstract: Materials exhibiting noncollinear magnetism or strong spin-orbit-coupling underpin many spintronic and topological applications, but their simulations require complex two-component spinors and costs substantially more than scalar density functional theory (DFT). We present a GPU-centric exascale finite-element DFT framework with noncollinear magnetism and spin-orbit-coupling, combining (1) adaptive higher-order finite-element discretization; (2) a matrix-free Poisson solver; (3) residual-based Chebyshev filtered subspace iteration (R-ChFSI) for sparse generalized eigenproblems; (4) R-ChFSI-enabled mixed-precision computation with block floating-point compressed MPI communication; and (5) communication-efficient band partitioning. R-ChFSI permits inexact matrix-multivector products and 4x–6.4x compression of communicated data relative to FP64 while preserving double-precision robustness and reducing computation and data movement. Results demonstrate strong scaling on Aurora and Frontier, with up to 3.4x faster Chebyshev filtering. On Aurora, total self-consistent-field (SCF) solve wall time reduces by 2x. An 800-node (9,600-GPU) calculation demonstrates fully relativistic pseudopotential DFT for ~80,000 electrons in under seven minutes per SCF iteration.

records.title: TempGNN: An Efficient Real-Time TGNN Inference Accelerator via Target-Centric Dependency Packets
records.abstract: Temporal graph neural networks (TGNNs) effectively model dynamic graphs, but inference suffers from limited useful parallelism and irregular memory accesses because strict temporal dependencies require timestamp-ordered vertex updates. We present TempGNN, a target-centric accelerator for high-performance real-time TGNN inference. TempGNN reorganizes sampled temporal computation into target dependency packets (TDPs), each capturing the minimal temporally valid dependency states required to update a target vertex. By decoupling dependency preparation from ordered target-state commitment, TempGNN preserves temporal correctness while exposing branch-level parallelism across partially overlapping targets. To realize this execution model, TempGNN integrates a dependency-driven TDP construction and data-loading scheme together with an overlap-aware synchronization strategy that eliminates redundant dependency processing and supports efficient on-chip execution. Implemented on a Xilinx Alveo U280 FPGA, TempGNN achieves 28.2× speedup and 33.5× energy savings over an A100 GPU, and further delivers 3.8×–7.6× speedups with 6.5×–10.2× energy savings over prior TGNN accelerators.

records.title: BTC-TC: Exact GPU Triangle Counting with Hybrid Bit Tensor Cores and CUDA Cores
records.abstract: Triangle counting is fundamental to graph analytics, yet GPUs face a tension between exact, irregular adjacency-list intersection and regular, inaccurate FP16 Tensor Core execution. ToT's FP16 pipeline is incorrect on 12 of 36 inputs and requires pre-kernel symbolic matching. We observe that semantic alignment alone is insufficient under heterogeneous mask density. We present BTC-TC, an exact system built around binary MMA. AND-popcount implements common-neighbor counting with 32-bit accumulation and enables online block matching. Because mask density varies, BTC-TC combines multi-granularity Bit-BSR with two-level adaptivity: it selects block geometry per graph, dispatches dense blocks to Bit Tensor Cores, and routes sparse blocks to CUDA cores. Across 36 inputs and 12 baselines on RTX PRO 6000, BTC-TC achieves the lowest post-clean end-to-end time on every input, with 1.92x geometric-mean kernel and 8.0x end-to-end speedups over ToT. It matches CPU ground truth on every input and maintains the gains on H100 and A800.

records.title: Parallel k-Clique Counting via Hierarchical Breadth-First Search
records.abstract: We propose a new parallel algorithm for k-clique counting, a fundamental primitive in graph analytics. The state-of-the-art algorithm combinatorially counts k-cliques within maximal cliques to reduce the search tree size. However, its parallel performance degrades rapidly with clique size, due to (1) wasted work exploring subproblems that contain no k-cliques, and (2) load imbalance from highly irregular subproblem sizes. We introduce a hierarchical BFS-based algorithm, Calico, that restricts the search to a reduced edge set. To mitigate load imbalance, Calico also limits search tree depth by reformulating dense subproblems as counting independent sets on their corresponding complement graphs. Calico achieves up to 16,631× speedup over parallel baselines with scaling up to 192 cores on large real-world graphs. Calico is the first to count k-cliques of any specified size on the previously intractable com-LiveJournal graph, reducing the reported runtime from approximately 62 hours (k ≤ 13) to under 14 seconds.

records.title: TriBIT: Triangle Counting Using Binary Tensor Core Operations
records.abstract: The graph triangle counting (TC) problem appears frequently in scientific computing domains such as large-scale graph processing, bioinformatics or social network analysis, motivating the need for efficient TC techniques on HPC platforms. However, existing approaches deliver suboptimal end-to-end performance due to (1) high memory consumption; (2) expensive graph preprocessing overheads; and (3) substantial data movement across heterogeneous CPU-GPU platforms. To overcome these problems, we propose TriBIT, the first TC algorithm for GPUs that (1) leverages bitmap-based compressed data structures particularly tailored to the TC problem, significantly reducing memory footprint; and (2) exploits bitwise operations in GPU Tensor Core Units (TCUs). On single-GPU scenarios, using 810 sparse graphs from the SuiteSparse Matrix Collection, TriBIT achieves geometric mean speedups ranging from 4.63× to 213.61× over state-of-the-art approaches. In multi-GPU scenarios, TriBIT processes graphs with more than 128 billion edges, achieving a throughput of 381 billion triangles per second on 32 GPUs.

records.title: OctoPipe: Reducing Pipeline Bubbles for Heterogeneous Models via Co-Optimizing Partitioning, Placement, and Scheduling
records.abstract: Pipeline parallelism is widely used to train large language models (LLMs). However, increasing heterogeneity in model architectures exacerbates pipeline bubbles. Prior approaches typically optimize a single phase of the pipeline schedule (i.e., partitioning, placement, or scheduling), leaving substantial bubbles. While promising, co-optimization poses three key challenges: (1) complex performance modeling, (2) a combinatorial search space, and (3) irregular execution orders. We propose OctoPipe, a pipeline parallelism system to co-optimize partitioning, placement, and scheduling. First, we build a graph-based pipeline simulator to model heterogeneous pipeline execution for co-optimization. Second, we develop an iterative bubble-aware tuner to efficiently explore the combinatorial search space. Third, we implement a unified pipeline executor that dynamically orchestrates computation and communication to support irregular execution orders without deadlocks while maximizing communication-computation overlap. Experiments show that OctoPipe achieves 1.09x-1.49x throughput improvement over the state-of-the-art pipeline parallelism approaches across various heterogeneous model configurations and GPU cluster scales.

records.title: REAL: Efficient Distributed Training of Dynamic GNNs with Reuse-Aware Load Balancing Scheduling
records.abstract: Dynamic graph neural networks (DGNNs) enable learning from evolving graphs by capturing both structural and temporal dependencies. However, scaling DGNN training remains challenging due to three conflicting objectives: maximizing resource utilization, minimizing data movement, and maximizing data reuse. Existing systems typically optimize one objective at the expense of the others, leading to communication bottlenecks, load imbalance, or redundant computation. We present REAL, an efficient distributed system for DGNN training that jointly addresses these challenges. REAL minimizes data transfers through snapshot-group scheduling and introduces an incremental aggregation mechanism that decouples computation from structural updates, enabling snapshot- and group-level reuse to eliminate redundant I/O and FLOPs. We further design two complementary schedulers: Real-L, an ILP-based optimizer for globally optimal planning, and Real-G, a scalable greedy heuristic. Experiments on six dynamic graph datasets and four DGNN models show that Real-L and Real-G achieve up to 3.26× and 3.16× speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.

records.title: BatchFlow: Benefit-Aware Data Pipeline Allocation and Batch Reuse for Multi-Job Training
records.abstract: Deep learning training is often limited by data pipeline throughput, reducing accelerator utilization and increasing training time and cost. This is particularly challenging in multi-tenant environments, where jobs compete for storage and CPU resources. We present BatchFlow, a data pipeline service that improves aggregate training throughput by dynamically allocating data pipeline workers across jobs. BatchFlow uses online profiling to estimate how quickly each job consumes mini-batches and how quickly workers can prepare them, then allocates workers to jobs where data supply is most likely to fall behind training demand. BatchFlow also caches prepared mini-batches for reuse across jobs, reducing repeated reads from slow storage and redundant CPU preprocessing. When cache capacity is limited, a benefit-aware policy determines which mini-batches to prefetch and retain. Across multi-job workloads, BatchFlow increases aggregate training throughput by up to 3.8× and cost efficiency by up to 2.1× relative to prior systems.

records.title: Ordered Chaos: Towards Adaptive Multipath Load Balancing with Precise, Fast Loss Detection
records.abstract: Load balancing in best-effort datacenter fabrics faces a trade-off. Order-preserving schemes such as equal-cost multipath (ECMP) retain loss semantics but use path diversity coarsely, while packet spraying balances load well but removes the ordering signals needed for fast, precise loss detection. We present Ordered Chaos, an end-host design that preserves enough structure for reliable loss detection without giving up fine-grained multipath routing. Reactive subflow spraying (RSS) divides each flow into ordered, dynamically routed subflows. Precise fast loss detection (PFLD) combines this ordering with probes to distinguish reordering from congestion, corruption, tail, and retransmission losses within one RTT. Across simulations, AI and HPC workloads, and a DPU prototype, RSS+PFLD improves tail flow completion time by up to 3x, eliminates up to 99% of timeout-based recoveries, and accelerates collective and training communication by up to 35%.

records.title: Format-Driven Automatic Pipeline Construction and Load Balancing for SpMM on GPUs
records.abstract: Sparse matrix-dense matrix multiplication (SpMM) is critical for graph neural networks, yet GPU optimization faces challenges from irregular sparsity and thread-block load imbalance. Existing hand-tuned solutions tightly couple format design with kernel implementation, requiring reimplementation when the format changes. We present Sparsene, a format-driven automated framework that derives all kernel-level optimizations from a single sparse format specification. A hierarchical DSL decouples format structure from implementation via declarative blocking primitives and dynamic lowering transformations. The frontend compiles the DSL into a pGraph of pTasks, whose granularity and dependencies are determined by the format. This format-derived pGraph drives both automatic pipeline construction, where a hardware-aware simulator and two-stage hybrid search identify high-quality pipeline plans, and format-aware load balancing, which selects among binding strategies through per-input profiling to mitigate thread-block load imbalance. Experiments on NVIDIA A100, H100, and RTX 4090 demonstrate up to 8x speedup over state-of-the-art solutions with performance portability.

records.title: From Alert Fatigue to Root Cause: Causal Failure Cascade Discovery in HPC Systems
records.abstract: Production HPC systems generate massive volumes of heterogeneous logs that encode rich signals about failure propagation across hardware and software layers. In this paper, we present a framework for causal discovery in HPC logs that combines three complementary methods: transformer-based counterfactual intervention, PCMCI+, and transfer-entropy. Because production environments lack labeled ground truth, our framework uses cross-method triangulation to assign confidence to discovered causal relationships. We further introduce an architecture-aware AI-agent that evaluates the physical plausibility of these relationships and enriches them with mechanism-level explanations, diagnostic commands, and severity assessments grounded in Frontier system documentation. We apply the framework to 18.4 billion log events from the Frontier supercomputer and construct a structured taxonomy of 87 event types spanning diverse hardware and software subsystems. Our results reveal causal relationships across HPC-subsystems, including rare failure pathways and multi-hop cascade chains. This work provides a scalable path toward architecture-grounded root-cause diagnosis in production HPC-systems.

records.title: Sensor Placement for Tsunami Early Warning via Large-Scale Bayesian Optimal Experimental Design
records.abstract: Real-time tsunami early warning relies on distributed sensor networks to infer seismic sources and seafloor motion. Optimizing these networks via Bayesian optimal experimental design (OED) is exceptionally challenging for systems governed by hyperbolic partial differential equations, which lack the spectral decay required by standard low-rank approximations. We present a scalable Bayesian OED framework for linear time-invariant systems. By reformulating the inverse problem in the data space, we transform OED into dense matrix subset selection. We propose a multi-GPU, Schur-complement-update-based, greedy algorithm that solves the OED problem using a pipelined approach that fully overlaps I/O with GPU computations. Our framework achieves near-perfect weak and strong scaling across hundreds of GPUs on Perlmutter and Frontier. Applied to the 2025 Gordon Bell Prize-winning digital twin for tsunami forecasting in the Cascadia Subduction Zone, we optimize a 175-sensor network, minimizing the uncertainty of a parameter field with over one billion degrees of freedom.

records.title: MatterScale: Scaling Foundation Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Billion-Atom Molecular Dynamics on the Next-Generation Supercomputer
records.abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials have enabled molecular dynamics with ab initio accuracy at greatly reduced cost and at large scale. The field is now shifting toward foundation machine learning interatomic potentials with broader transferability, but these models are harder to scale because message-passing layers complicate distributed communication and two-body and three-body features increase graph-construction cost and memory footprint. We present MatterScale, an end-to-end framework for deploying foundation MLIPs on massively parallel molecular dynamics workloads on a next-generation supercomputer. MatterScale combines a Halo operator for nearest-neighbor inter-layer feature exchange, an ML-based multiple-time-step scheme for higher throughput, layer-wise activation checkpointing for higher per-node capacity, and a parallel graph-construction algorithm. With MatterSim, MatterScale scales to 32,768 GPGPUs with 94% weak scaling efficiency and simulates up to 1.13 billion atoms.

records.title: Star-LAFT: An Agent-Driven Adaptive Framework for Fault-Tolerant High-Throughput Materials Informatics
records.abstract: High-throughput computational materials science workflows execute millions of simulations on HPC clusters to build materials genome databases for data-driven discovery. However, these workflows face critical challenges: complex task dependencies reduce scheduling efficiency, load imbalances waste resources, and parameter-sensitive simulations suffer poor fault resilience. We present Star-LAFT, an agent-driven framework integrating large language models (LLMs) for automated workflow construction, dynamic resource optimization, and multi-level fault recovery. Key innovations include: (1) LLM-based automatic inference of computational parameters from material specifications; (2) chain-of-thought-driven dynamic resource allocation; and (3) a hybrid fault-tolerance agent that pairs an LLM diagnoser with a reward-guided recovery-action selector. Benchmarks show Star-LAFT achieves a 2.12× wall-time speedup and 10.08% higher task completion with only 2.76% additional cost. At production scale (~300k materials), it generated a million-entry database in 10 weeks at 94.3% completion rate, enabling effective downstream AI model training.
