records.title: Trigger, Render, Reason: Multimodal LLM Agents for Science-Aware Scientific Simulation Monitoring
records.abstract: Scientific simulations on leadership-class HPC systems routinely waste millions of core-hours producing invalid results, yet no tool monitors whether a running simulation computes valid science. We call this blind spot dark waste. Detecting it requires physics-aware judgment at every timestep, which neither humans nor system-level monitors supply. Multimodal LLM agents could, but they cannot ingest scientific data: no field fits in a context window. What an agent can ingest is a rendering, a lossy encoding that discards precision, preserves structure, and stays a fixed size regardless of the field behind it. Because a fixed rendering answers only the question it was made for, we give the agent control of the visualization. Vigil instantiates this as a trigger-render-reason pipeline: cheap deterministic triggers watch every timestep, and only flagged states are rendered and reasoned over. Across four codes, Vigil detects every parameter-induced failure and dismisses a trigger fired on a healthy run.

records.title: DiffSpec: Accelerating Long Sequence Generation with Differential Speculative Decoding
records.abstract: Long sequence generation is a critical workload for large language model (LLM) inference, but its high computational cost limits scalable deployment. Existing speculative decoding methods accelerate inference by verifying multiple draft tokens per step, yet uniform speculation concentrates failures in late decoding stages, where marginal payoff is highest, reducing overall speedup. We propose DiffSpec, a differential speculative decoding framework that adapts speculation to position-specific utility. At the algorithmic level, DiffSpec employs utility-guided draft construction with relevance-aware key-value (KV) selection and adaptive draft tree construction, improving candidate quality in high-impact regions. At the system level, a differential speculative execution engine supports utility-adaptive speculation via reuse-aware KV residency and topology-aware fused verification, handling irregular KV cache accesses and heterogeneous workloads. Experiments on four NVIDIA H100 GPUs with sequences up to 128K tokens show end-to-end speedups of 7.72×, 3.45×, and 2.36× over EAGLE-3, TriForce, and MagicDec, respectively.

records.title: Spec-K: Adaptive Resource Allocation via Speculative Preview for Efficient MoE Inference
records.abstract: Inference serving for large language models (LLMs) often relies on static resource allocation—such as fixed Top-k routing in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models—despite substantial token-level heterogeneity. This mismatch causes systematic over-provisioning, magnified in long reasoning and batched speculative decoding. We introduce Resource Allocation via Speculative Preview (RASP), a framework that leverages predictive signals from a draft model to guide token-level allocation before target-model verification, enabling fine-grained adjustment of compute budgets to match instantaneous demand. As an instantiation, Spec-K applies RASP to MoE routing: it uses speculative preview to estimate token uncertainty and reallocates the Top-k budget dynamically via a minimalist policy, reducing expert computation, communication traffic, and activated expert count in batched verification—thereby improving throughput and even speculative acceptance. Experiments on distributed MoE inference show that Spec-K achieves up to 1.72× end-to-end throughput improvement over a strong baseline, with negligible accuracy loss on complex reasoning and instruction-following tasks.

records.title: TIDE: Temporal Incremental Draft Engine for Self-Improving LLM Inference
records.abstract: Speculative decoding can substantially accelerate LLM inference, but realizing its benefits in practice is challenging due to evolving workloads. We present TIDE (Temporal Incremental Draft Engine), a serving-engine-native framework that integrates online draft adaptation directly into high-performance LLM inference systems. TIDE reuses target model's intermediate hidden states generated during inference as training signals for draft adaptation, thereby avoiding additional target model computation and serving-time overhead. It employs adaptive runtime control to activate speculation and draft model training only when beneficial. TIDE exploits heterogeneous clusters by mapping inference and training to appropriate GPU classes. Across diverse real-world workloads, TIDE achieves up to 1.66× throughput over no-speculation baselines while recovering performance on misaligned workloads where static draft models degrade throughput. TIDE also reduces training time by up to 3.02× and storage requirements by 24× compared to existing draft training approaches, and improves system throughput by up to 1.22× on heterogeneous GPU clusters.

records.title: LLMProf: Identifying Performance Bottlenecks in LLM Serving Systems with Top-Down Profiling
records.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving systems have become critical cloud workloads, yet their performance diagnosis remains challenging due to rapid software-hardware evolution, dynamic request patterns, and the limitations of existing profiling tools. These gaps force developers to rely on manual heuristics for performance optimization, leading to slow progress and error-prone code. We present LLMProf, a low-overhead profiling framework tailored for various LLM serving systems. LLMProf employs a top-down, multi-level analysis approach that captures only the most relevant metrics at each profiling level to balance detail with minimal performance impact while remaining agnostic to frameworks and hardware. We present case studies that leverage LLMProf to optimize real-world LLM serving workloads, from which we derive a performance diagnosis taxonomy that provides actionable guidance and enables automated postmortem analysis. Our case studies demonstrate that by applying simple optimizations uncovered by LLMProf, we can achieve up to 2.09× throughput improvement.

records.title: What Bloats Your Floats? Right-Sizing Numerical Precision for Scientific Computing
records.abstract: While FP64 (binary64) remains the standard representation of real numbers in scientific computing, hardware trends increasingly favor low-precision formats optimized for AI workloads. This shift prioritizes throughput and energy efficiency over full-precision capabilities. We challenge the necessity of high-precision arithmetic in PDE-governed simulations, where spatial and temporal discretization errors introduce a physical noise floor that masks the lower-order bits of the FP64 format, rendering them irrelevant. We propose a criterion based on the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) with respect to spatial and temporal refinements to evaluate the impact of safe precision reduction on scientific computations. Finally, we present an automated dataflow-centric workflow for targeted lowering within mixed-precision subgraphs in complex scientific applications. Large-scale evaluations of weather and climate applications show that strategic precision reduction on GPUs achieves up to 1.8× speedup without compromising physical fidelity.

records.title: LLM Agents Meet Lossy Compression: Benchmark, Demystify, and Optimize Across HPC Architectures
records.abstract: LLM coding agents can resolve many repository-level issues, yet their ability to translate and optimize performance-critical HPC kernels across heterogeneous accelerators remains underexplored. Existing benchmarks conflate two distinct capabilities: generating correct target-platform code (translation) and improving throughput under correctness constraints (optimization). We present SZ-BENCH, a benchmark that separates these abilities for scientific lossy compression across CUDA, HIP, and Cerebras, covering nine kernels and five applications. Evaluating four LLM backbones and two agentic workflows, we find large performance variation on GPUs, systematic failure on PE-centric Cerebras targets, and persistent tension between correctness and throughput. Additional reasoning iterations often degrade results. To address these issues, we propose SZ-GEN, a multi-agent workflow that integrates generation, profiling, and validation. SZ-GEN achieves up to 30.05/190.32 GB/s on SZp/CUDA, significantly outperforming baselines, though requiring more search iterations.

records.title: Scalable High-Fidelity Macromolecular Docking for GPU-Accelerated Supercomputers
records.abstract: Flexible macromolecular docking offers high-fidelity predictions of biomolecular interactions, but remains prohibitively expensive at scale. Among existing approaches, LightDock leverages glowworm swarm optimization (GSO) for accuracy, yet suffers from limited parallelism, irregular computation, and severe load imbalance, preventing efficient execution on GPU supercomputers. We present SparkleDock, a scalable GSO-based docking framework enabling near-real-time flexible docking. We redesign GSO to expose massive fine-grained parallelism at the glowworm-agent level, and restructure the dominant energy scoring computation into a Tensor Core-compatible formulation, enabling efficient execution of irregular pairwise interactions through structured matrix operations. We further introduce a performance-model-driven scheduling for load balancing and out-of-core scaling across GPUs. SparkleDock achieves 9.7× and 18.9× speedups over LightDock on single A100 and H100 GPUs, and delivers over two orders of magnitude acceleration at scale. On 512 GPUs, it reduces docking time from hours to seconds, enabling large-scale, high-fidelity virtual screening previously impractical with flexible docking.

records.title: Bridging Precision and Performance Gaps: Scientific Computing on AI-Oriented Architectures
records.abstract: The rapid rise of AI-oriented accelerators has reshaped compute systems around low-precision tensor engines, raising a practical question for the HPC community: Under what conditions can such hardware support scientific workloads that demand numerical robustness, irregular memory access, and scalability? Using the Ascend 910 NPU series as a representative tensor-centric platform, we characterize precision, execution, and memory-hierarchy bottlenecks that hinder the direct deployment of scientific codes. From this characterization, we develop and evaluate workload-specific mappings that combine heterogeneous execution, mixed-precision numerical formulations, hierarchical memory orchestration, and communication–computation overlap. Evaluations spanning kernels, numerical solvers, quantum simulation, and Monte Carlo applications show that AI-native NPUs can achieve numerical robustness, competitive performance, and satisfactory scalability when these constraints are addressed in a coordinated manner. Our results provide a state-of-the-practice case study of how scientific workloads can be adapted to tensor-centric architectures, while distinguishing transferable optimization principles from Ascend-specific implementation details.

records.title: Scaling Quantum Circuit Optimization via Guided Exploration and Global Context Learning
records.abstract: Every circuit gate in a quantum program can add execution errors on noisy quantum hardware, making gate-count reduction important for reliable quantum computing. Rule-based optimizers use greedy search and miss improvements requiring long rewrite sequences. Learning-based methods are promising but constrained by incomplete circuit representations, unfocused exploration, and poor scalability. To address these limitations, we introduce GUIDERQ, a new reinforcement-learning optimizer with three key advances: combining local and global circuit features for richer representations, learned filtering to focus on the most promising candidate actions, and recursive partition-and-reassembly that scales to large circuits while exploring optimization opportunities across partitioning boundaries. Across representative quantum-circuit benchmarks with up to 27,883 gates and three industry-standard gate sets, GUIDERQ achieves geometric-mean gate-count reductions of 33.0%, 34.2%, and 25.1% on the IBM, Nam, and TDG gate sets — up to 34.1% more than Quarl, the state-of-the-art learning-based optimizer — with up to 3× faster search.

records.title: Park-n-Ride: Hardware-Aware Compilation and Execution of Bivariate Bicycle Codes on Neutral-Atom Systems
records.abstract: Quantum computers are noisy; without quantum error correction (QEC), deep programs fail as qubits lose information due to decoherence. Among QEC approaches, bivariate bicycle (BB) codes offer low overhead and constant-depth syndrome extraction, while neutral-atom arrays provide scalable, reconfigurable qubit layouts. However, executing BB-code primitives on neutral-atom systems requires a hardware-aware mapping that respects movement, zoning, and interaction constraints. We present Park-n-Ride, a system for compiling and executing the BB code on neutral-atom processors. Park-n-Ride introduces a module layout and movement model aligned with neutral-atom constraints, exposes a compact BB-native logical interface for compilation, and integrates scheduling mechanisms that enable efficient execution on zoned architectures. By co-designing BB-code abstractions with hardware execution, Park-n-Ride provides a practical path from qLDPC primitives to resource-efficient, high-throughput execution on reconfigurable neutral-atom arrays.

records.title: BAHAMAS: A Control Plane for Optimization and Execution of Variational Quantum Circuits
records.abstract: Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) suffer from unstable optimization due to temporal noise drift and static qubit mappings that distort gradient signals across iterations. We present BAHAMAS, an online control framework that stabilizes noise exposure by adaptively selecting physical mappings via consensus-based fidelity estimation, without requiring simulators, offline training, or prior executions. Across real quantum devices, BAHAMAS improves optimization reliability and supports inference-time retargeting under drift through robust, per-iteration control.

records.title: QPAR: A Plug-In Parallel Framework for Qubit Routing
records.abstract: Qubit routing, a key stage of quantum compiler, inserts additional operations (e.g., SWAP gates) to ensure quantum circuit instructions are executable on physical hardware. The effectiveness of routing in terms of minimizing additional operations is critical, as they introduce extra overhead and noise. However, existing routing methods often suffer from high computational overhead, limiting their scalability for large-scale circuit compilation. To overcome this limitation, we present QPAR, a plug-in parallel framework to boost the scalability of routing algorithms. The key insight of QPAR is that, while qubit routing is a sequential process, we can first relax the sequential dependencies to enable parallelism and then rebuild them to ensure correctness. QPAR further establishes optimizations to combat potential loss of routing effectiveness caused by parallelization. Experimental results demonstrate that QPAR can accelerate routing algorithms by up to 126.6x, with negligible, even negative, cost increases on a 128-logical-core server.

records.title: TETRIS-Q: Tiling-Based Effective Transient-Fault Reduction on Interleaved Superconducting Qubits
records.abstract: The struggle of the hour in quantum computing research is achieving effective suppression of the error mechanisms induced by the interaction of external radiation with superconducting quantum devices. Despite the rapid advancements in quantum error correction (QEC) of recent years, radiation-induced faults are yet to be fully addressed. These events are known to be the cause of simultaneous correlated defects in qubits that lie onto a single substrate, ultimately annulling QEC code effectiveness. In this paper, we propose to selectively combine substrate-level phonon barriers and QEC interleaving via a planar-mesh tiling algorithm, TETRIS-Q, reaching efficient and effective suppression of radiation events. Our cross-layer solution comes at no extra cost in terms of QEC code execution or decoding time. We model and simulate radiation-induced transient faults over a plethora of barrier and QEC interleaving configurations.

records.title: The Anatomy of a Misprediction: Tracking Terrestrial and Orbital Radiation-Induced Errors in Systolic Arrays
records.abstract: The increasing use of systolic arrays to accelerate AI in safety-critical domains, such as autonomous vehicles and space systems, makes their reliability a primary concern. Existing approaches often analyze the impact of faults at a single abstraction level, failing to capture how radiation-induced events at hardware level translate into system-level failures. This gap limits the ability to identify which hardware faults lead to critical application errors and to design effective mitigation strategies. To address this challenge, we propose a cross-layer analysis that traces faults from their origin in silicon to their impact on AI models. By exposing tensor processing units to accelerated terrestrial and orbital radiation environments (neutron and proton beams) and combining hardware-level simulations with software-level fault injection, we identify error patterns and propagation mechanisms that result in mispredictions. This end-to-end perspective enables the identification of the low-level sources of errors that lead to critical failures.

records.title: BitIR: Cross-Architecture Fault Injection for Resilience Analysis of Heterogeneous GPU Applications
records.abstract: Modern GPU-based HPC systems rely on heterogeneous vendor stacks, yet reliability studies are largely limited to single architectures. Consequently, it remains unclear how faults behave across different GPU backends. We present BitIR, a cross-architecture fault injection framework that enables semantically aligned, software-visible resilience analysis across NVIDIA, Intel, and AMD GPUs. BitIR injects deterministic faults at the LLVM IR level, ensuring equivalent bit perturbations prior to backend lowering and enabling direct cross-vendor comparison. Using a set of representative GPU benchmarks, we conduct large-scale injection campaigns on production systems and classify outcomes into masked results, silent data corruption (SDC), failures, and hangs. We find that identical faults produce markedly different behaviors across vendors: Intel most often masks faults but exhibits more hangs when faults escape masking; NVIDIA exposes more overt detectable failures; and AMD alternates between SDC-dominant and failure-dominant behavior depending on the benchmark and fault site.

records.title: GPU Faults Across Cloud Providers: Characterization and Operational Insights at Scale
records.abstract: Reliability is a critical challenge in operating large-scale GPU training infrastructure across multiple cloud providers. Despite growing interest in GPU fault characterization, no prior work describes the automated systems that manage faults across providers at scale, nor a methodology for continuous reliability improvement. We operate a large GPU training fleet spanning all major CSPs and NCPs, encompassing various GPU architectures with close to 1 billion GPU hours/year. We focus on three production clusters at the highest maturity level (≥98% node availability) across three providers, analyzing 19,564 fault incidents across 5,065 nodes over 5–7 months. To maintain availability, we built a breakfix system with three pillars: scale-up automation, fault triage with provider-specific remediation actions, and repeat-offender management. We report on reliability KPIs: mean time to repair (MTTR), automated triage success rate (ATSR), node recidivism rate (NRR), and present a Pareto-driven methodology for continuous improvement.

records.title: LLM-PRISM: Characterizing Silent Data Corruption from Permanent GPU Faults in LLM Training
records.abstract: Large-scale LLM training is increasingly susceptible to hardware defects stemming from manufacturing escapes and silicon aging. These defects manifest as silent data corruption (SDC) that perturbs gradients and parameters throughout the training process. We present LLM-PRISM, a methodology to characterize LLM pre-training resilience to hardware faults. LLM-PRISM couples RTL-level GPU fault simulation with a stochastic injection engine embedded in Megatron-LM. Through 7,664 training runs across FP16, BF16, and FP8 regimes, we analyze how fault type, rate, and numeric format govern resilience. We find that while LLMs resist low-frequency faults, impact is highly non-uniform; critical datapaths and specific precision formats can induce catastrophic divergence even at moderate fault rates. This study provides the first hardware-grounded, pre-training characterization of SDC resilience.

records.title: COPPER: Improving DRAM Reliability with Low Overheads via Cooperative Parallelized Error-Correcting Codes
records.abstract: DRAM scaling increases fault rates, motivating stronger and more efficient error correction. However, the transparency between on-die ECC (OD-ECC) in DRAM and rank-level ECC (RL-ECC) in the memory controller introduces substantial storage, reliability, and performance overheads. We propose COPPER, a cooperative ECC mechanism that improves reliability with low performance and area overheads. COPPER exploits the fixed mapping between DRAM data arrays and interface pins to convey a crafted error-location hint from OD-ECC to the memory controller, enabling parallel rank-level cross-checking and decoding without stalling memory transfers. We further propose POD-RMW, which provably parallelizes OD-ECC operations during read-modify-write. Our evaluations show that COPPER incurs only 0.007% DRAM-chip area and at most 0.001% CPU area. With 19.5% storage overhead, COPPER reduces DUE and SDC rates by up to 15x and 430x, respectively, while improving performance by up to 2.1x over prior cooperative ECC approaches under high fault rates.

records.title: Temporal Modeling of Soft Error Propagation Using Dynamic Bayesian Networks
records.abstract: With the ever-shrinking size of transistors, modern devices have become increasingly susceptible to soft errors that can lead to silent data corruption (SDC), seriously compromising system reliability. Understanding how these corruptions propagate through a program's execution is essential for accurate resilience analysis, yet existing analytical models rely on static assumptions that miss temporal behavior, while fault-injection studies reveal only final outcomes without exposing the intermediate propagation paths. This paper introduces Hydra, a temporal error-propagation framework that constructs a dynamic Bayesian network (DBN) from the program execution trace to model how corrupted values traverse dataflow, control-flow, and memory-dependency transitions. Hydra captures masking, reactivation, multi-step propagation, and long-range dependencies, enabling estimation of program-level SDC probabilities without repeated injections and revealing interpretable propagation pathways. Across a diverse benchmark suite, Hydra's predicted SDC probabilities closely match fault-injection results, achieving a mean absolute error of 2.2 percentage points, while substantially reducing computational cost.

records.title: Low-Overhead Silent Error Detection for Large Language Model Inference at Scale
records.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely deployed across large-scale computing systems, where soft errors can silently corrupt computations and degrade output quality. Existing protection techniques often rely on broad monitoring or expensive checking mechanisms, incurring non-negligible runtime overhead and limiting scalability across architectures and workloads. In this work, we propose TRACE, a lightweight fault-detection technique for generative LLMs. TRACE identifies a small set of critical layers that are most informative under fault conditions, places lightweight activation-based symptom monitors on these layers during inference, and uses a trained model to determine whether a fault has corrupted the generated output. Across 15 LLMs and three datasets, TRACE achieves 95.3% average fault-detection coverage with only 0.56% runtime overhead, a 6.1× reduction relative to prior LLM fault-tolerance techniques. TRACE further remains effective under multi-bit faults and multi-dataset profiling, demonstrating robust detection across diverse fault conditions and workloads.

records.title: PHANTOM: Phase-Aware Power Management for Energy-Efficient LLM Training
records.abstract: GPUs enable large-scale LLM training, but high energy consumption and sharp power transients hurt efficiency and reliability. Existing GPU power-management methods are largely reactive and do not exploit the phase structure of training iterations. We present PHANTOM, a predictive, phase-aware dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) framework for sustainable and reliable multi-GPU LLM training. We show that iteration-level power traces exhibit repeatable, fine-grained phase patterns. PHANTOM uses a lightweight temporal convolutional network (TCN) to predict short-horizon GPU power from synchronized hardware events and phase signals, then applies a Pareto-based multi-objective optimizer to choose frequencies ahead of phase transitions, balancing energy efficiency and power stability under real-time constraints. This design is lightweight enough for online deployment without intrusive changes to the training workflow. On multi-GPU LLM workloads, PHANTOM reduces energy by 15%–16%, normalized power-slew rate (NPSR) by 9%–15%, and energy–delay product (EDP) by 10%–11% compared with the default hardware DVFS policy.

records.title: Scalable and Efficient Simulation of LLM Training
records.abstract: Simulation offers unique values for both enumeration and extrapolation purposes, and is becoming increasingly important for managing the massive machine learning (ML) clusters and large-scale distributed training jobs. In this paper, we build Echo to tackle three key challenges in large-scale training simulation: (1) tracing the runtime training workloads at each device in an ex-situ fashion so we can use a single device to obtain the actual execution graphs of 1K-GPU training; (2) accurately estimating the collective communication without high overheads of discrete-event-based network simulation; and (3) accounting for the interference-induced computation slowdown from overlapping communication and computation kernels on the same device. Echo supports both dense and MoE workloads with high fidelity and further enables GPU memory-aware ex-situ simulation. Echo delivers on average 8% error in training step (~3x lower than state-of-the-art simulators) for GPT-175B on a 256-GPU H800 cluster with 3D parallelism on Megatron-LM under three minutes.

records.title: Cross-Layer Energy Analysis of Multimodal Training on Grace Hopper Superchips
records.abstract: Multimodal deep learning jointly processes text, images, and video, but scaling models and sequences shifts training bottlenecks from computation toward memory capacity and data movement. DeepSpeed addresses these limits through CPU offloading, activation checkpointing, and sequence parallelism, yet these techniques add communication and system activity that can alter energy efficiency. We present a cross-layer study of multimodal training on NVIDIA Grace Hopper (GH200) systems, characterizing interactions among the application, runtime, and hardware layers. Using controlled experiments across multiple model scales, we evaluate power, energy, runtime, and throughput under offloading and parallelism strategies. Results show that energy efficiency depends primarily on data movement and compute-communication overlap rather than raw accelerator utilization; consequently, runtime-optimal configurations are not always energy-optimal. We derive practical guidelines for selecting offloading modes, sequence-parallelism degrees, and hardware-aware schedules that balance memory pressure, communication cost, time-to-solution, and energy on tightly coupled heterogeneous systems.

records.title: Characterizing the Scalability and Performance of Large-Scale AI Training Under Multi-Tenancy
records.abstract: Characterizing AI workload performance on modern HPC systems requires understanding both their scalability in isolation and their behavior under concurrent execution. However, the interplay among parallelization strategies, network congestion, compute capability, and interconnect technologies remains poorly understood. This work investigates the performance and scalability of AI models up to 2,400 GPUs. We quantify the communication overheads and their impact across different interconnects by evaluating scale-up, scale-out, and rack-scale configurations under multiple allocation schemes. Finally, we study how multiple concurrent training jobs interfere with each other by designing a realistic noise model. We design a benchmark suite of AI models to evaluate the performance of five distinct parallelization strategies across different supercomputing clusters, including Alps, Leonardo, LUMI, JUPITER, NVL72 GB300, and DGX A100. Our work provides a systematic characterization of the scalability and execution efficiency of distributed AI training, while offering key insights into performance behavior under realistic multi-tenant scenarios.

records.title: Wafer-Net: A Flexible Hierarchical Interconnection Architecture Based on Wafer-Scale Integration
records.abstract: High-performance interconnection networks are typically built upon high-radix routers. As system scale continues to grow, the conventional switch-centric scaling paradigm faces severe challenges in latency, deployment cost, and scalability. This paper proposes Wafer-Net, a flexible hierarchical interconnection architecture enabled by wafer-scale integration. Wafer-Net abstracts distributed on-wafer compute and switch resources into two composable building blocks—the Compute Chiplet Group (CCG) and the Switch Chiplet Group (SCG)—and thereby recasts conventional interconnection networks as a hierarchical structure that combines local high-bandwidth domains with global low-latency switching. We further propose a formal mapping framework based on hierarchical compression transformations and dynamic programming. Using this framework, we instantiate three representative Wafer-Net topologies, which significantly reduce network diameter and cabling overhead while supporting concise and efficient minimal/non-minimal and adaptive routing algorithms. Simulation results show that these Wafer-Net topologies consistently outperform both their conventional counterparts and the wafer-scale baseline in throughput and latency.

records.title: Scalable Generation of Distributed-Memory Mappings for Large Tensor Networks
records.abstract: Large-scale tensor networks are a critical class of computations widely used in domains such as computational chemistry, machine learning, and others. Owing to their memory footprint and complexity, their execution requires distributed-memory clusters and deeply efficient communication. This work proposes an enhanced non-linear formulation that unifies previously proposed modeling and optimization schemes for DAGs of tensor operators. Our new modeling and formulation finds high-performing mappings for large tensor networks. Our key scientific contribution is a novel representation of the hyper-dimensional grid of processing elements. The new abstraction exponentially expands the search space, yielding higher performance and enhanced scalability. Furthermore, we reformulate the mapping to exploit optimization procedures in Google CP-SAT, leading to over 50x scalability improvement relative to prior work. We evaluate our approach on various DAGs targeting CPU and multi-GPU clusters. Our approach achieves average speedups of 4.01x and 1.73x over the Cyclops Tensor Framework and NVIDIA cuTensorNet, respectively.

records.title: GLOW: Accelerating Geometric Multigrid Layers on Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine
records.abstract: This paper describes the mapping of geometric multigrid (GMG) onto the Cerebras Wafer Scale Engine (WSE-3). The WSE wafer integrates almost a million cores along with a low-latency 2D mesh network, providing unprecedented on-chip bandwidth and fine-grained communication. Although the architecture is predominantly used for deep learning, we explore the suitability of WSE for accelerating GMG. GMG solves sparse linear systems efficiently by recursively coarsening the grid, which leads to more rapid convergence with less computation. As compared to prior implementations of stencils on WSE, this demonstration highlights the challenges of mapping a layered algorithm – and the full set of operators – onto a dataflow architecture. We compare the performance of this implementation to that of the HPGMG benchmark on an NVIDIA GH200 GPU. Across different GMG configurations and problem sizes, we observe a speedup of up to 25× as compared to a single GH200 node.

records.title: SpaDA: A Spatial Dataflow Architecture Programming Language
records.abstract: Spatial dataflow architectures like the Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine deliver exceptional performance in AI and scientific computing by distributing scratchpad memory across hundreds of thousands of processing elements (PEs). Yet programming these architectures remains difficult: with no shared memory, data movement requires explicit configuration, and asynchronous task management introduces substantial complexity. We present SpaDA, a programming language that offers precise control over data placement, dataflow patterns, and asynchronous operations while abstracting low-level architectural details. We design and implement a compiler targeting Cerebras CSL through multi-level lowering and unique optimization passes. SpaDA functions as a high-level programming interface and an intermediate representation for domain-specific languages (DSLs), demonstrated here with the GT4Py stencil DSL. SpaDA enables concise expression of operations with complex parallel patterns — including collective operations, multi-dimensional stencils, dense and sparse linear algebra — in 7.49× fewer lines than CSL, achieving over 260 TFlop/s across 730,000 PEs on a single device.

records.title: OCEAN: Open-Source CXL Emulation for Hyperscale Architecture and Networking
records.abstract: Compute Express Link (CXL) 3.0 introduces fabric-level memory pooling, yet the absence of production CXL 3.0 hardware and the complexity of multi-host configurations pose significant barriers to the research community. This paper presents OCEAN, a high-fidelity, open-source emulation framework that reproduces the fabric-level feature set that distinguishes CXL 3.0—including multi-host memory sharing, dynamic capacity management, and coherent pooling across hosts—using QEMU virtualization and custom Linux kernel modules. OCEAN makes two central technical contributions: active latency injection and a software cache coherence layer implementing MESI-state management with distributed snoop filters to maintain correctness across up to 16 hosts. We validate OCEAN against a real CXL Type-3 device. In addition, case studies on Tigon database workloads quantify the throughput impact of hardware cache coherence—an 11× improvement at full coverage—while a design-space sweep of 12 memory-placement policies on GROMACS demonstrates up to 7% performance variation from policy choice alone.

records.title: TPage: Transparent Page Management for CXL-Based Tiered Memory Systems
records.abstract: The emerging Compute Express Link (CXL) technique introduces critical management challenges in tiered memory systems, particularly the trade‑off between data migration overhead and memory space efficiency. A 4KB‑based page unit enables fine‑grained memory management but incurs high migration latency and high page table scan overhead. 2MB‑based transparent huge page (THP) improves the migration efficiency but often wastes significant memory space due to the underutilized page space. To resolve the problem, we propose TPage, a transparent page management framework for CXL‑based tiered memory systems. TPage enables four key innovations: (1) PMU‑assisted memory imbalance monitor, (2) two‑phase page table scan, (3) hybrid page hotness tracking, and (4) huge-page‑aware page placement. TPage dynamically monitors inter‑node memory access pressure imbalance and proactively migrates pages to mitigate it. These mechanisms collectively reduce memory bloat and accelerate page migration, speeding up the performance by 3.6× over Transparent Page Placement (TPP).

records.title: Quantifying the Cost of Software-Managed Synchronization on Multi-Host CXL Memory
records.abstract: Current multi-host CXL platforms provide shared, byte-addressable memory, but no cross-host cache coherence or atomic operations. As a result, the main challenge is not remote-memory latency itself, but the software overhead required to ensure visibility and synchronization. We quantify this overhead on a real four-host CXL shared-memory system, covering raw memory performance, software-managed publish/observe visibility, and synchronization built from explicit flushes and polling. On our platform, one-way cross-host visibility is about 1 µs, and each lock acquisition costs 3–5 µs, roughly an order of magnitude higher than local hardware spin locks. These overheads dominate synchronization-heavy workloads: BFS gains nothing from adding a second host; it requires frequent barriers and cross-host exchange. In contrast, triangle counting, which is read-dominated with little synchronization, does speed up when scaling from 32 to 32+32 threads across two hosts. Overall, suitability depends on remote-write intensity, synchronization frequency, and whether hot metadata stays in local DRAM.

records.title: Towards High-Performance Sparse Graph Attention on Dense Tensor Core Units
records.abstract: Sparse graph attention (SGA) is a critical building block of attention-based graph neural networks (GNNs). Existing approaches either optimize individual primitives (e.g., SDDMM or SpMM) in isolation or rely on block-sparse representations, which fail to map graph-sparse workloads efficiently onto dense TCUs. We propose SpG-Attention, a unified framework that bridges sparse graph attention with dense TCU computation. Specifically, SpG-Attention introduces: (1) memory-efficient SGA (ME-SGA) parallel strategies that classify attention multiplications by their reduction characteristics and choose row/column-wise parallelization accordingly; (2) a TCU-friendly condensed-sparse format and customized fused kernels with MMA-aligned tiled execution, discrete-to-contiguous tiled loading, metadata prefetch pipelining, and register-fragment alignment; and (3) input-aware runtime optimizations based on graph statistics and refined by bounded online profiling to handle structural diversity and long-tail degree distributions. Extensive experiments on real-world graphs demonstrate that SpG-Attention achieves average speedups of 2.45x over Fused3S for inference and 2.15x over FlashSparse for end-to-end training.

records.title: Distributed Variational Quantum Linear Solver
records.abstract: VQLS is a promising hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for solving linear systems Ax=b, but its practical deployment is hindered by the massive circuit execution overhead required when encoding arbitrary matrices via linear combination of unitaries (LCU) decomposition. Evaluating the VQLS cost function requires quadratic scaling requirement with the LCU terms, resulting in tens of thousands of circuits per iteration and millions of executions across a full optimization trajectory. To address this, we present a scalable, distributed implementation of VQLS that exploits the embarrassingly parallel structure of the gradient-free-based cost function using NVIDIA CUDA-Q conjunction with multi-node distribution for HPC system. Benchmarking on the Perlmutter supercomputer, we validated the VQLS algorithm with a sample tridiagonal Toeplitz and a canonical Hele-Shaw fluid flow problem. Furthermore, we demonstrate near ideal strong scaling and high efficiency weak scaling performance. We also used Nsight to benchmark the distributed framework to explore ideal concurrency.

records.title: ZenKO: Guided and Iterative Quantum-Classical Method for Molecular Electronic Structure Using Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization
records.abstract: The electronic structure of molecules is foundational for scientific advancement; however, determining it remains challenging due to the growth of the molecular Hilbert space with system size. Recent approaches address this by using quantum circuits to sample candidate configurations and sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) to compute the ground state. We propose ZenKO, a novel gradient-based, iterative SQD method that employs a hybrid quantum-classical approach. ZenKO decomposes configuration selection into discovery, validation, and refinement, enabling targeted subspace expansion and guided exploration. Our evaluation demonstrates that, across H₂O, H₁₀, and N₂ molecules, ZenKO improves ground-state accuracy compared to prior iterative methods, while significantly reducing classical cost.

records.title: Quantum Sampling Architecture for Protein Structure Reconstruction on Utility-Scale Hardware
records.abstract: Predicting the structure of short peptides in protein binding pockets remains difficult: the regime requires physics-based conformational search, yet no existing method performs that search practically on current hardware. We present QSAD, a quantum-classical framework that reformulates peptide structure prediction as amino-acid-level Hamiltonian sampling and replaces iterative optimization with non-iterative Hamiltonian evolution. Executed entirely on IBM Heron R2 across 101 binding-pocket peptides (5-18 residues), QSAD improves prediction accuracy by 27%-71% over all evaluated AI and quantum baselines, with the lowest variance across tested lengths. QSAD also tolerates noise levels 3x-5x beyond typical hardware error rates, where iterative methods fail, and achieves a mean per-case speedup of 27x in quantum execution time relative to VQE. The sampled ensemble further supports approximate reconstruction of protein energy landscapes. These results establish coarse-grained quantum sampling as a practical path for structure prediction where data-driven methods lack sufficient signal.

records.title: BatchMine: Accelerating Approximate Graph Pattern Mining via Batch Processing
records.abstract: Approximate graph pattern mining, as a fundamental technique in graph analysis, has been widely applied in machine learning, biomedical research, and social network analysis. However, existing solutions still face significant challenges in efficiency and scalability when dealing with complex pattern graphs or giant data graphs. To address these limitations, we introduce BatchMine, an out-of-core system for approximate graph pattern mining. BatchMine leverages three key techniques: (1) a partition-based estimation method to accelerate convergence; (2) a batch-processing framework with adaptive refinement to enhance external-memory access locality and improve convergence efficiency; and (3) a hybrid data layout that balances sampling efficiency and storage overhead. To the best of our knowledge, BatchMine is the first graph pattern mining system capable of handling graphs exceeding main memory capacity, enabling mining on graphs with nearly 100 billion edges on a single machine within 1,000 seconds. Extensive experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of BatchMine.

records.title: KSPine: Fast Parallel K-Shortest Path Computation via Block-Cut+ Tree Decomposition and Dynamic Caching
records.abstract: Efficiently computing K-shortest path (KSP) on graphs is critical for many real-world applications. Existing solutions suffer from query-dependent pruning, limited parallelism, and redundant computation across repeated queries. To address such challenges, this paper presents KSPine, a fast parallel KSP framework. KSPine is built on block-cut+ tree (BC+ tree), a structural decomposition that identifies a compact, query-independent skeleton of the graph using biconnected components and articulation points. This skeleton allows KSPine to prune each query to a small structural subgraph and solve independent sub-KSP problems within each BiCC block in parallel. To combine local sub-KSP results into global top-K paths, we design a merging-based method with early stopping that reduces unnecessary computation. KSPine also introduces a hierarchical dynamic caching mechanism that reuses sub-KSP results across queries, avoiding redundant computation under continuous workloads. On six real-world graphs across various domains, KSPine achieves an average speedup of 1.5× over state-of-the-art methods.

records.title: PUMatch: Bandwidth-Efficient DFS-Based Subgraph Matching Under GPU Memory Oversubscription
records.abstract: Subgraph matching on massive graphs is hindered by GPU memory oversubscription, where frequent CPU-GPU data transfers create severe performance bottlenecks. Existing unified memory solutions suffer from bandwidth waste due to coarse-grained page transfers, while BFS-based approaches often fail due to intermediate result explosion. To address these challenges, we present PUMatch, a bandwidth-efficient, DFS-based CPU-GPU collaborative framework. PUMatch introduces four key innovations: (1) dual-scale packaging that reorganizes missing neighborhoods into compact CSR units to maximize bandwidth efficiency; (2) a synchronization-free asynchronous coordination protocol for DFS execution; (3) orthogonal warp scheduling with trie-based resumption that operates independently of the SM’s built-in scheduler; and (4) an adaptive hybrid data access scheme that dynamically optimizes data movement via a lightweight learning controller. Extensive experiments on real-world graphs with billions of edges demonstrate that PUMatch achieves up to 10.49× speedup over state-of-the-art BFS baselines and 3.45× over DFS baselines, while reducing PCIe traffic by 73%.

records.title: BMS2: Fast Batched Subgraph Matching on GPUs with Structure-Aware Scheduling
records.abstract: Batched matching is widely used in drug discovery, software analysis, and social network analysis. Its core operation, subgraph matching, is an NP-complete graph algorithm that has been optimized in the HPC field for decades. As for batching scenario, we find that current subgraph matching systems are unable to leverage the common structure patterns of real-world graphs, thereby missing potential optimization opportunities. In this paper, we propose BMS2, a batched matching system with structure-aware scheduling. BMS2 incorporates these intrinsic properties into previous general filter-join strategy: (1) in the filter phase, BMS2 utilizes the presence information of special structure for early termination; (2) in the join phase, we exploit the similarity of batched queries to reuse matching results of common structure. Experiments demonstrate that BMS2 can achieve an order of magnitude performance improvement on GPUs compared to the state-of-the-art with the ability to process two orders of magnitude larger dataset.

records.title: Practical HPCQC Integration with QDMI: A Real-Hardware Case Study with IQM Systems
records.abstract: Quantum computers are entering HPC centers, shifting the main challenge from hardware access to integration. Many software paths still rely on vendor-specific adapter chains between user SDKs, schedulers, and backend APIs, which complicates operations and slows the move from pilots to production. We present a practical integration path built on the Quantum Device Management Interface (QDMI). Using IQM superconducting systems as a hardware case study, we implement an IQM-backed QDMI layer and connect it to two software layers HPC centers already care about: Slurm-based job execution and Qiskit-facing user workflows. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/iqm-finland/QDMI-on-IQM. The message is that integrating quantum hardware into HPC need not be a bespoke effort per backend. Once the software–hardware boundary is standardized, large parts of the stack become reusable across providers and deployment styles. We do not claim that this removes all HPCQC challenges, but that this boundary can be standardized today.

records.title: End-to-End Modeling and Trace-Driven Replay for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Supercomputing
records.abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical applications increasingly execute as multi-stage workflows spanning HPC nodes, simulators, workflow runtimes, network services, and remote quantum backends. Evaluating such applications is difficult because their end-to-end critical path crosses heterogeneous components with incompatible observability and control interfaces, making reported results hard to reproduce, compare, and extrapolate. We present QTrace, an end-to-end methodology for performance analysis of hybrid quantum-classical workloads. QTrace combines a unified cross-layer tracing schema with a dependency-aware, trace-driven replay engine that preserves workflow causality while enabling controlled perturbation of backend latency, scheduling policy, and reliability-related effects. This supports both faithful reproduction of observed executions and systematic "what-if" studies for future quantum-accelerated systems. We evaluate QTrace on representative iterative and adaptive workloads across simulator-backed and remote-backend settings. The results show that QTrace reconstructs workflow behavior with high fidelity, reproduces observed executions with low replay error, and exposes bottlenecks that are often hidden by backend-centric metrics alone.

records.title: A GPU-Accelerated and Geometry-Aware Quantum-Classical Framework for Optimized PES Scans with CUDA-Q
records.abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical workloads, particularly potential-energy-surface (PES) scans in quantum chemistry using batched VQE and QAOA, involve many structurally similar Hamiltonians differing only in coefficients. Existing warm-start and meta-optimization strategies reuse parameters between instances but still fixed quantum-classical resources, ignoring cross-instance structural similarities. We present OptiPESS, a GPU-accelerated runtime system for adaptive resource allocation in hybrid quantum-classical execution. OptiPESS introduces the Locality-Occupancy-Variance (LOV) metric, a lightweight, geometry-aware measure of Hamiltonian similarity, coupled with efficient alignment and Pauli-classification passes. Using LOV, OptiPESS performs distance-aware scheduling of iteration and shot budgets, predicting which instances can be skipped, quick-solved, or fully optimized. Implemented atop CUDA-Q with persistent multi-GPU execution and near-linear scaling, OptiPESS reduces classical and quantum evaluations by up to 78.3% and wall-time by up to 74.8% while maintaining baseline accuracy. This demonstrates how lightweight static analysis and adaptive scheduling can transform quantum-classical co-execution from fixed-budget loops into a predictive, resource-aware runtime.

records.title: Toward Continental Forest Dynamics Modeling at Individual-Tree Resolution on Exascale Systems
records.abstract: Modeling continental-to-global forest dynamics at individual-tree resolution is essential for Earth system prediction but has remained computationally impractical because of cross-scale interactions among billions of trees in heterogeneous atmospheric and soil environments. We present GGap, an agent-based forest model designed for exascale systems. GGap employs a Site–Gap–Tree hierarchy that co-locates each site's ensemble on a single GPU to maximize data locality. It leverages two-level parallelism: site partitions run concurrently across MPI ranks, while GPU threads update agents within each rank. To avoid CPU–GPU synchronization, a multi-priority kernel pipeline executes sequential ecological phases entirely on-device, using grid barriers to enforce their order. On Frontier, the largest weak-scaling configuration simulates 10.25 billion agents on 2,048 GPUs at 96.2% parallel efficiency. A 1,000-year contiguous United States simulation across 1,424 sites and 235 species reproduces regional patterns of species composition, forest structure, productivity, and biomass, demonstrating ecologically meaningful continental-scale forest simulation.

records.title: Demonstrating the Neuromorphic Advantage on Stochastic Dynamics in Turbulent Flows
records.abstract: Graphics processing units (GPUs) excel at workloads dependent on linear algebra, covering a wide range of topics like artificial intelligence and quantum mechanics. However, in workloads that are not well captured by linear algebra, such as probabilistic systems, GPUs may not provide optimal performance. In this work, we demonstrate a neuromorphic advantage in energy efficiency for simulating turbulent flows with stochastic methods. We observe energy savings across the board and runtime speed-up for some methods when comparing a neuromorphic platform to equivalent workloads on GPU and CPU. Specifically, our neuromorphic implementation achieves 1.52x speed-up and 37.46x less energy consumption, compared to a GPU running the same 1.5 million random walks over discretized space. For 100,000 walks in continuous space, GPU outperforms neuromorphic in execution time but consumes 2.37x more energy. As the technological landscape for neuromorphic systems rapidly evolves, their performance relative to current hardware is likely to significantly improve.

records.title: MakoXC: Rearchitecting DFT Exchange–Correlation with Matrix-Aligned and Knowledge-Organized Sparsity
records.abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) is essential to materials science and drug discovery, yet exchange–correlation (XC) evaluation remains a major bottleneck. Linear-scaling methods exploit electronic nearsightedness but introduce irregular sparse workloads that underutilize modern AI accelerators. We present MakoXC, a matrix-aligned XC engine that restructures nearsightedness-induced sparsity into regular accelerator-friendly computation. MakoXC combines matrix-aligned cells to organize interactions into dense clusters, sparsity-guided activation to expose implicit sparsity for practical linear scaling, and a kernel-fused pipeline to consolidate fragmented workloads into a compute-intensive execution path. MakoXC achieves average speedups of 67.8x over standard XC evaluation and 4.7x over state-of-the-art linear-scaling methods. Integrated into a production-grade commercial DFT package, MakoXC scales to ubiquitin (1,231 atoms, def2-SVP) on 64 GPUs, completing end-to-end DFT in under five minutes. MakoXC demonstrates how scientific workloads can achieve genuine low complexity while maximizing parallel efficiency on AI accelerators.

records.title: From PME to FMM: A Modern Approach to Long-Range Force Calculation in GROMACS
records.abstract: The fast multipole method (FMM) is a potentially scalable method for long-range electrostatics in molecular dynamics (MD) codes such as GROMACS. Most MD codes have relied for decades on the highly optimized particle mesh Ewald (PME) method, but its reliance on fast Fourier transforms introduces all-to-all communication that ultimately limits strong scaling, whereas FMM uses a hierarchical communication pattern in which farther nodes exchange less information. In this study, we tightly integrate a highly-scalable and GPU-accelerated FMM into GROMACS, which for the first time shows an actual advantage over PME in time-to-solution. We compared both FMM and PME on the ALPS cluster across one to 128 Grace Hopper compute nodes, each equipped with four NVIDIA GH200 GPUs, over multiple MD test systems. Across these systems, including a 44-million-atom simulation, our FMM implementation shows markedly better scalability than GROMACS' highly optimized PME implementation and achieves up to 2.57× speedup at scale.

records.title: HSTUFuse: Training-Compatible Efficient Fusion for Long-Sequence Recommenders
records.abstract: Generative recommenders improve the modeling of long-range behavioral dependencies through unified causal sequence modeling, where the hierarchical sequential transduction unit (HSTU) serves as a core sequence encoder. However, the original HSTU implementation incurs fragmented operator execution, cross-feature reductions in LayerNorm, padding overhead from dense materialization, and redundant spatial aggregation. We present HSTUFuse, a training-compatible CUDA optimization that decomposes HSTU into three stages—pointwise projection, spatial aggregation, and pointwise transformation—with fused forward and backward implementations. It further replaces LayerNorm with Dynamic Tanh, internalizes jagged-tensor addressing, and combines valid-position computation with causal lower-triangular pruning. ML-1M training runs show stable convergence while retaining recommendation quality close to the PyTorch HSTU. On ML-20M, it achieves per-batch HSTU execution speedups of 19.53× on RTX 4090 and 22.46× on H800, measured using the sum of forward- and backward-pass times.

records.title: FitFloat: Read/Write Random-Access Compressed Floating-Point Arrays for GPUs
records.abstract: In many floating-point applications that use GPUs, device memory is a bottleneck limiting the maximum problem size. One solution is to use Unified Virtual Memory, but the limited physical GPU memory likely causes page evictions, incurring potentially large performance penalties. We present FitFloat, a drop-in floating-point array replacement supporting user-specified precision on GPUs with the goal of reducing storage requirements of scientific applications while maximizing performance over unified memory. FitFloat targets applications limited by the GPU's memory capacity, allowing larger problem sizes to be efficiently processed. We evaluate the storage savings and performance improvement of our approach relative to using native arrays on 11 single-precision and three double-precision codes from the HeCBench suite on two different GPUs. In the best case, FitFloat yields a speedup of 739 and provides a geometric-mean speedup of 16.1 for the float codes and 20.1 for the double codes on an RTX 4090.

records.title: Chisa: Dynamic Logical Way Partitioning for Efficient Caching in Sparse Accelerators
records.abstract: Sparse tensor computations are memory-bound, making on-chip data reuse critical to sparse accelerator performance. Guided cache replacement derives lookahead information from structural relationships between operand tensors, but its effectiveness hinges on the prefetch observation window in SRAM. Under constrained SRAM, the window is inevitably small and guidance becomes noisy or misleading—precisely when caching matters most. We propose Chisa, a dynamic logical way partitioning scheme for sparse accelerator caches. Inspired by victim caches, Chisa integrates buffer semantics into cache sets: a single role bit lets each way dynamically serve as a logical cache or buffer way without data migration, so mistakenly evicted blocks can be rescued upon reuse. Chisa further incorporates Jaccard similarity-based initialization and rescue rate-based runtime adaptation. On real-world sparse matrices, Chisa achieves geometric mean speedups of 1.23x and 1.27x over the state of the art on SpMSpM and SpMM, respectively, peaking at 4.46x and 4.64x.

records.title: High-Performance Tensor Formulation of the Viterbi Algorithm for Hidden Semi-Markov Models
records.abstract: Hidden semi-Markov models (HSMMs) are fundamental probabilistic models widely adopted across diverse domains, from computational biology to finance and signal processing. The Viterbi algorithm decodes the most likely state sequence given an HSMM and can be applied iteratively for ab initio model learning. However, existing Viterbi implementations remain sequential, and GPU-accelerated solutions are entirely absent, making HSMM decoding impractical for large-scale workloads. We present a tensor-based formulation of the Viterbi algorithm for HSMMs, restructuring the inner loops into tensor operations that naturally map onto SIMD units and massively parallel architectures. Building on this formulation, we provide optimized implementations spanning single- and multi-core CPUs, and, for the first time, GPU. Experimental evaluation demonstrates speedups of up to 14× on a single core, over 200× with multi-core, and over 570× on GPU over the state-of-the-art sequential baseline, establishing a new performance baseline for large-scale HSMM decoding.

records.title: PIMCQG: Co-Designing Billion-Scale Graph-Based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search for Processing-in-Memory
records.abstract: Graph-based approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) delivers superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs for large-scale AI applications, but remains fundamentally bottlenecked by the ”memory wall” on CPUs and GPUs. Processing-in-memory (PIM) offers massive internal bandwidth by co-locating computation with data, making it a natural fit for irregular, memory-bound workloads. However, directly mapping graph-based ANNS onto PIM exposes severe algorithm–architecture mismatches: restricted per-PU memory, costly inter-PU communication, heavy coordination overhead, and weak compute capability, forcing existing PIM-based ANNS to rely on cluster-based algorithms that plateau at low recall. We propose PIMCQG, an algorithm–hardware co-design framework through three optimizations: (1) a compact index reducing PIM-resident footprint by 14.5×; (2) an asynchronous pipelined scheduler fully utilizing host–PIM bandwidth; (3) a multiplication-free distance kernel with <0.08% recall loss. Evaluations on three billion-scale datasets show up to 20×/17.1× throughput over CPU/GPU baselines, 129× over prior PIM accelerators at high recall, and scale across multi-node and emerging PIM architectures.

records.title: FluxZK: Scalable and Efficient Zero-Knowledge Proof Computation via GPU Acceleration
records.abstract: Zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) protocols enable privacy-preserving verification but face critical performance bottlenecks at the proof generation stage, particularly when handling large-scale computations that exceed GPU memory capacity. We present FluxZK, a framework that addresses scalability and efficiency challenges through ZKP-specific GPU-based optimizations. Our framework introduces FluxMSM, an efficient multi-scalar multiplication (MSM) implementation that leverages fine-grained parallelism and overlapped data transfer with computation. Additionally, we develop FluxNTT, a high-performance number theoretic transform (NTT) solution supporting both out-of-core and on-GPU computation paradigms. Extensive evaluations on data center GPUs demonstrate that FluxZK scales well to large input sizes of up to 2³⁰ elements, delivering an estimated performance improvement of up to 2.16x over existing solutions in real-world ZKP applications. Our code is open-sourced at https://github.com/SJTU-Liquid/FluxZK.

records.title: MPCAR: Scalable and Secure Multi-Party Computation-Based AllReduce
records.abstract: Scalable and secure collective communication is critical in modern HPC and AI workloads, especially AllReduce. State-of-the-art (SOTA) solutions use homomorphic encryption (HE) to ensure data privacy, but incur complex key management and overheads, and weak integration with collective algorithms. We present MPCAR, the first multi-party computation-based AllReduce framework, which decouples AllReduce into two phases, data reduction and distribution, and applies tailored secure methods to each. MPCAR employs secret sharing MPC schemes for the data reduction phase and asymmetric one-time-padding-based protection for the distribution phase, while also allowing user-defined secure communication protocols. We co-design these schemes with multiple AllReduce algorithms and implement several system-level optimizations. Evaluated across five platforms spanning AWS and HPC clusters at scale, including two exascale supercomputers and scaling to 8,192 ranks, MPCAR improves latency/throughput by up to 30.5%/41.2%. MPCAR also outperforms SOTA by up to 21.3% on real-world workloads, including DNN applications and three DeepSeek-distilled models.

records.title: eFaaS: A Lightweight, Kernel-Bypass Serverless Framework for HPC Workloads
records.abstract: HPC workflows are growing in scale and complexity, demanding elastic resource provisioning and fine-grained parallel execution. While serverless computing is conceptually well-suited due to its on-demand model, existing frameworks are primarily designed for lightweight, event-driven workloads, leading to fundamental mismatches in highly concurrent HPC scenarios. In such workloads, large numbers of function instances must be created simultaneously, introducing significant startup and communication overhead. Kernel-dependent mechanisms—such as cgroups, namespaces, and the network stack—become bottlenecks: instance initialization triggers heavy lock contention, while cross-node communication incurs additional costs from data copying, serialization, and context switching. To address these issues, we propose eFaaS, a serverless architecture tailored for HPC. By leveraging eBPF, eFaaS enables lock-free isolation and zero-copy communication, minimizing kernel overhead. Experimental results show that eFaaS maintains stable performance under extreme concurrency, significantly reduces long-tail latency, and achieves end-to-end speedups of 1.27×–3.74× across representative HPC workflows.

records.title: Beyond Screen Time: Inferring Everyday Life Context from Diverse Smartphone Data
records.abstract: Smartphones serve as ubiquitous sensors of daily life, generating rich data streams. However, existing research often focuses narrowly on usage metrics from small or homogeneous samples, limiting our understanding of how phone data reflects broader real-world contexts. To address this gap, this paper introduces a hierarchical context inference framework designed to systematically map raw and multimodal data into two deep contextual dimensions: the Informational-Cognitive Context and the Physical-Situational Context. We empirically validated this framework through a large-scale, 14-day in-the-wild study involving a diverse cohort ( N = 539) spanning 15 occupations and 31 provincial regions in China. Applying our framework to this data reveals generalizable phenomena: the information environment frequently mixes multiple topics, shows high emotional fluctuation, and exhibits task-driven volatility rhythms. Physically, users own diverse Bluetooth peripherals but show focused usage, and our models reveal stable and cyclical phone interaction patterns across distinct operational states. Integrating these dimensions yields nuanced user personas that differ across occupational, hobby, and personality groups. This work contributes a validated framework for understanding the interplay between users' digital and physical worlds, supported by the release of a comprehensive multimodal dataset.

records.title: SIGMA-ASL: Sensor-Integrated Multimodal Dataset for Sign Language Recognition
records.abstract: Automatic sign language recognition (SLR) has become a key enabler of inclusive human-computer interaction, fostering seamless communication between deaf individuals and hearing communities. Despite significant advances in multimodal learning, existing SLR research remains dominated by vision-based datasets, which are limited by sensitivity to lighting and occlusion, privacy concerns, and a lack of cross-modal diversity. To address these challenges, we introduce SIGMA-ASL , a large-scale multimodal dataset for SLR. The dataset integrates an Azure Kinect RGB-D camera, a millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar, and two wrist-worn inertial measurement units (IMUs) to capture complementary visual, radio-reflection, and kinematic information. Collected in a controlled studio environment with 20 participants performing 160 common American sign language (ASL) signs, SIGMA-ASL provides 93,545 temporally synchronized word-level multimodal clips. A unified sensing framework achieves millisecond-level alignment across modalities, enabling reliable sensor fusion and cross-modal learning. We further design standardized preprocessing pipelines and benchmarking protocols under both user-dependent and user-independent settings, offering a comprehensive foundation for evaluating single and multimodal SLR. Extensive experiments validate the dataset's quality and demonstrate its potential as a valuable resource for developing robust, privacy-preserving, and ubiquitous sign language recognition systems.

records.title: MAGIC: A Dataset Capturing Mid-Air Gesture Performance for Interaction and Feature Analysis
records.abstract: Mid-air gestures are increasingly used as a natural modality in interactive systems, ranging from smart home controls and automotive interfaces to augmented reality and public displays. Despite their growing adoption across diverse domains, we still lack a comprehensive understanding of what makes gestures effective, expressive, and robust across participants and application domains. We conducted a data collection study in which we captured a novel dataset of 18 widely used mid-air gestures, each performed by 42 participants. A total of 4,265 gesture samples were recorded using synchronized electromagnetic sensors and depth cameras. We analyzed gestures using kinematic and geometric measures, and quantified consistency in terms of hand shape and palm trajectory using Multidimensional Dynamic Time Warping. We further trained LSTM-based classifiers as recognition baselines and computed a deep-feature consistency measure from their learned embedding space. Results revealed that consistency and recognizability vary substantially across gesture types, and consistency scores were positively associated with recognition performance. These findings provide empirical guidance for the design and selection of mid-air gesture vocabularies in real-world interaction systems.

records.title: Act2Intention: A Benchmark For Developing Active Mobile Agents Through Inferring User Intention From GUI Actions
records.abstract: Mobile GUI Agents powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show promise in human-computer intelligence. However, current research primarily focuses on reactive task execution while lacking a comprehensive “understanding-prediction-execution” process for user intentions, which are the core requirements of active agents. In this paper, we propose the Act2Intention framework that builds an active mobile agent by integrating understanding, predicting user intentions, and executing decisions. Firstly, we constructed the Act2Intention Bench through collection and validated generation, comprising 72,511 intentions and over 700,000 actions across 52 apps, thereby establishing the first benchmark for evaluating proactive agents via continuous “intention-actions” trajectories. We further develop the Act2Intention Agent, achieving proactive services through Proactive-oriented Intention Understanding, Personalized Proactive Intention Prediction, and Experience-guided Intention Execution. Experimental results show that supervised fine-tuning on Act2Intention Bench yields absolute improvements of +32.0 Acc-S, +10.25 Acc-S, and +6.9 SSR points over non-fine-tuned counterparts under the same agent framework for intention understanding, prediction, and execution, respectively. This success underscores the necessity and value of the Act2Intention Bench, which establishes a standardized platform for developing and evaluating proactive agents and consequently paves the way for research on intention-driven human-computer interaction. To facilitate further research, we open-source our code and Act2Intention Bench at: npuNancy/Act2Intention.

records.title: Models Got Talent: Identifying High Performing Wearable Human Activity Recognition Models Without Training
records.abstract: Discovering high performing model architectures for wearables-based Human Activity Recognition (HAR) applications is challenging. The astonishing diversity and variability due to differing sensor locations, recording apparatus, activities, etc., can cause established architectures to perform worse on datasets/tasks they were not designed for. A promising complement to Neural Architecture Search (NAS) involves the development of Zero Cost Proxies (ZCPs), which correlate well with trained performance, but can be computed through a single forward/backward pass on a randomly sampled batch of data. In this paper, we investigate the effectiveness of eight ZCPs on six benchmark HAR datasets, and demonstrate that the top-predicted architectures obtain performance within 7% of that attained by full-scale training of 2,000 randomly sampled architectures. Furthermore, training the top-10 predicted architectures results in performance within 2% of full-scale training, leading to substantial computational savings. Our experiments introduce ZCPs to sensor-based HAR and demonstrate their suitability as an addition to NAS pipelines in practical scenarios.

records.title: XGait: A Multi-Modality Wireless Sensing Dataset for Indoor Human Tracking and Identification
records.abstract: Wireless sensing has emerged as a promising approach for tracking and identification using commodity Internet of Things devices. However, the features derived from a single wireless modality are often fragile to variations in environmental layouts and walking trajectories. Furthermore, most existing studies are based on datasets collected in specific scenarios with limited trajectory diversity and sensing modalities, preventing a robust evaluation of system generalization. To address this gap, we introduce XGait, a multi-modality wireless sensing dataset that synchronously captures human walking using Wi-Fi and acoustic transceivers across three indoor scenarios, with vision-based measurements serving as ground truth. Specifically, XGait contains more than 22K walking samples from 27 participants, covering diverse directions and trajectories to support both indoor tracking and identity recognition. To bridge the heterogeneity of wireless sensing modalities, we propose a unified Doppler spectrogram representation that maps Wi-Fi and acoustic signals into a shared time-frequency space, along with a standardized benchmark pipeline for pre-processing, temporal alignment, and feature construction, enabling reproducible evaluation and systematic cross-modal analysis. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that Wi-Fi and acoustic sensing exhibit complementary strengths, particularly under complex trajectories and challenging propagation conditions, thereby paving the way for novel research in the field of multi-modality wireless sensing. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/warrior-087/XGait.

records.title: M3PD Dataset: Enabling Dual-view Photoplethysmography on Smartphones in Lab and Clinical Settings
records.abstract: Portable physiological monitoring is essential for early detection and management of cardiovascular disease, but current methods often require specialized equipment that limits accessibility or imposes impractical postures that patients cannot maintain. Video-based photoplethysmography on smartphones offers a convenient non-invasive alternative, yet it still faces reliability challenges caused by motion artifacts, lighting variations, and single-view constraints. Few studies have demonstrated that this technology can be reliably applied to physiological monitoring of cardiovascular patients, and no widely used open datasets exist for researchers to examine its cross-device accuracy. To address these limitations, we introduce the M 3 PD dataset—the first publicly available dual-view mobile photoplethysmography dataset—comprising synchronized facial and fingertip videos captured simultaneously via front and rear smartphone cameras from 60 participants (including 47 cardiovascular patients). Building on this dual-view setting, we further propose the F 3 Mamba, which fuses the facial and fingertip views through Mamba-based temporal modeling. The model reduces heart-rate error by 21.9-30.2% over existing single-view baselines while showing enhanced robustness across challenging real-world scenarios, and further achieves a 4.4-16.4% MAE reduction over the best standard dual-view fusion baselines. Data and code are released at https://github.com/Health-HCI-Group/F3Mamba.

records.title: SpikeTouch: Optimizing Spike Neural Networks for Tactile Perception
records.abstract: Tactile perception enables systems to sense and interpret physical properties such as shape, material, pressure, and texture. It is a key capability for emerging applications like robotic surgery and assistive robotics. Existing solutions to tactile perception typically rely on computation-intensive deep neural networks, which require high-performance computing resources unavailable on embedded and battery-powered devices. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer a promising, energy-efficient alternative, but their practical adoption remains limited due to the lack of efficient and deployable neuromorphic solutions. We present S pike T ouch , a software framework designed to reduce the computational overhead of SNNs for tactile perception on neuromorphic hardware. S pike T ouch offers three key optimizations tailed to SNN-based tactile perception: (1) a spike encoding scheme that balances precision and computational cost; (2) a systematic method for extracting multidimensional tactile features; and (3) a training strategy that minimizes quantization errors to improve performance and reduce memory usage. We evaluate S pike T ouch on the Tianjic neuromorphic chip using representative tactile perception workloads. Our results show that S pike T ouch achieves high recognition accuracy for 30 objects and their material stiffness, with an average accuracy of 92.92% and 92.35%, respectively. It is also highly energy and computationally efficient, operating at just 1 Watt of power - significantly lower than the hundreds or thousands of Watts typically required by a GPU - and delivering a response in under 20 ms - well below the average human reflex time of over 100 ms.
